皇上御極之四年秋八月順天復
當大比士提調官府尹臣之

順天府鄉試錄序
皇上御極之四年秋八月，順天復當大比士。提調官府尹臣之垣、府丞臣南雍以請，上命中允臣洛文、贊善臣國爲考試官。既陛辭入院，則同考官進士臣一坤、臣應科、臣範，學正臣應鸞、臣承健，教諭臣洽、臣暘、臣應龍、臣燾、臣維鉉、臣世家，應聘咸集。臣乃用是歲禮官所條上科指，具相與毖飭以從事。而御史臣庭梧、臣一桂暨臣
translation_en:
Preface to the Record of the Shuntian Prefectural Provincial Examination

In the eighth month of autumn of the fourth year of His Majesty's reign [1576], it was again time for the triennial examination of scholars in Shuntian. Upon the petition of the Proctors, Prefectural Governor Your Servant [Wang] Zhiyuan 之垣 and Vice Governor Your Servant [Wang] Nanyong 南雍, His Majesty appointed Companion for the Heir Apparent Your Servant [He] Luowen 洛文 and Admonisher Your Servant [Xu] Guo 國 to serve as Examiners. After taking formal leave of the Throne and entering the examination compound, the Associate Examiners—Metropolitan Graduates (jinshi) Your Servants Yikun 一坤, Yingke 應科, and Fan 範; Department Directors of Studies Your Servants Yingluan 應鸞 and Chengjian 承健; and District Directors of Studies Your Servants Qia 洽, Yang 暘, Yinglong 應龍, Tao 燾, Weixuan 維鉉, and Shijia 世家—had all assembled in response to their invitations. We thereupon took the examination guidelines submitted item by item this year by the officials of the Ministry of Rites and together cautioned and admonished one another to carry out our duties accordingly. Meanwhile, Investigating Censors Your Servants Tingwu 庭梧 and Yigui 一桂, together with Your Servants…

title: 萬曆四年順天府鄉試錄
text:
李尚默臣曽士楚亦申明約
束譏防闌内外唯謹其諸執
事悉慎簡而祗役焉於是合
諸曹六館及提學御史臣傅
孟春所選士四千餘人三試
之遵
制額取百三十有五人并録其
===
文以
獻臣洛文嘗考覽古昔則人才
莫盛乎唐虞之際矣維其時
帝德光天之下故黎獻共臣
罔不敢應也聖人作而萬物
覩詎不信哉我
皇上紹熈洽之傳應中天之運

帝德光天之下故黎獻共臣
罔不敬應也聖人作而萬物
覩詎不信哉我
皇上紹熙洽之傳應中天之運
punctuated:
李尚默、臣曽士楚，亦申明約束，譏防闌内外唯謹，其諸執事悉慎簡而祗役焉。於是合諸曹、六館及提學御史臣傅孟春所選士四千餘人，三試之，遵制額取百三十有五人，并録其文以獻。
臣洛文嘗考覽古昔，則人才莫盛乎唐虞之際矣。維其時，帝德光天之下，故黎獻共臣，罔不敢應也。「聖人作而萬物覩」，詎不信哉！我皇上紹熈洽之傳，應中天之運，
translation_en:
… Li Shangmo 李尚默 and Your Servant Zeng Shichu 曽士楚 also reiterated the regulations and carefully inspected and guarded the interior and exterior of the examination compound, while all the various functionaries were prudently selected and respectfully performed their duties. Thereupon, combining the more than four thousand scholars selected by the various agencies, the Six Halls of the Directorate of Education, and Education-intendant Censor Your Servant Fu Mengchun 傅孟春, we tested them in three sessions. In compliance with the imperially decreed quota, we selected one hundred and thirty-five men, and also recorded their essays to present to the throne.

Your Servant [Chen] Luowen 洛文 has examined antiquity and found that men of talent were never more flourishing than during the era of Tang and Yu [Yao and Shun]. At that time, the sovereign's virtue illuminated all beneath heaven, and thus the eminent worthy men among the multitude all served together as ministers, none daring not to respond. "When the Sage arises, the myriad things behold him"—how could this not be true! Our August Emperor has inherited the succession of a prosperous and harmonious realm and answered the destiny of an era at high noon; …

title: 萬曆四年順天府鄉試錄
text:
聖神立極作民
君師海隅蒼生焜燿
明德既歷禩于兹矣爰自萬曆初
元即
俞言官請拓新試院至是規制秩
然始備間嘗
閔學官失職士習日偷申下
===
===
功令甚具屬肇舉
令典
臨幸辟雍縫掖之徒應薦来者靡
不獲與于橋門圜觀之盛而
典試之舉復
命臣等暫輟
講事以往蓋
alt_text:
聖神立極作民
君師海隅蒼生焜燿
明德既歷禩于茲矣爰自萬曆初
元即
俞言官請拓新試院至是規制秩
然始備閒嘗
閱學官失職士習日媮申下
===
功令甚具屬肇舉
令典
臨辛辟雍縫掖之徒應薦來者靡
不獲與于橋門圜觀之盛而
典試之舉復
命臣等暫輟
講事以往蓋
punctuated: 聖神立極，作民君師，海隅蒼生，焜燿明德，既歷禩于兹矣。爰自萬曆初元，即俞言官請，拓新試院，至是規制秩然始備。間嘗閔學官失職，士習日偷，申下功令甚具。屬肇舉令典，臨幸辟雍，縫掖之徒應薦来者，靡不獲與于橋門圜觀之盛。而典試之舉，復命臣等暫輟講事以往。蓋
translation_en: …With sacred and divine wisdom he has established the supreme standard, acting as the Ruler and Teacher of the people; the common folk to the corners of the seas have been illuminated by his resplendent virtue for several years now. From the very first year of the Wanli reign (1573), he approved the request of the speaking officials to expand and renovate the examination compound, and by now its layout and regulations are in orderly and complete array. In the meantime, concerned that educational officials were derelict in their duties and that the habits of scholars were growing daily more remiss, he repeatedly handed down detailed regulations for school evaluation. Recently, upon initiating the grand statutes, he visited the Imperial University in person, so that among the scholars in Confucian robes who had come in response to recommendations, there were none who did not get to share in the grand spectacle of surrounding the bridged gates to watch. And for the administration of the examination, he further commanded your servants to temporarily suspend our lecturing duties in order to go and preside. Truly, …

title: 萬曆四年順天府鄉試錄
text:
上之首重教化加意人才如此士
幸丁千載文明之會有不訢
然益奮者耶用是烝進羣髦
若棫樸芃芃然薪之槱之無
不可者而賢書豈勝載乎顧
臣茲不患多士之不充舉患
舉之而用或靡適不患錄者
===
之不文患文過而離其質也
何也敷納以言雖昉虞世然
所蘄者曰忠曰直足任股肱
耳目焉爾迨後科目制興亦
惟明當世之務習先聖之術
者是取蓋所為用之者固若
此也今世舉業之文日益侈
alt_text:

幸丁千載文明之會有不訏
然益奮者耶用是烝進羣髦
若棫樸芃芃然薪之槱之無
不可者而賢書豈勝載乎顧
臣
兹不患多士之不克舉患
舉之而用或靡適不患錄者
===
之不文患文過而離其質也
何也敷納以言雖昉虞世然
所蘄者曰忠曰直足任股肱
耳目焉爾逌後科目制興亦
惟明當世之務習先聖之術
者是取蓋所爲用之者固若
此也今世舉業之文日益侈
punctuated: 上之首重教化、加意人才如此。士幸丁千載文明之會，有不訢然益奮者耶？用是烝進羣髦，若棫樸芃芃然，薪之槱之，無不可者，而賢書豈勝載乎！顧臣茲不患多士之不充舉，患舉之而用或靡適；不患錄者之不文，患文過而離其質也。何也？敷納以言，雖昉虞世，然所蘄者，曰忠、曰直，足任股肱耳目焉爾。迨後科目制興，亦惟明當世之務、習先聖之術者是取，蓋所為用之者固若此也。今世舉業之文，日益侈
translation_en: … His Majesty places primary importance on moral transformation and pays special attention to men of talent in this manner. Scholars, fortunate to encounter this once-in-a-millennium era of flourishing culture, how could there be any who do not rejoice and rouse themselves all the more? For this reason, outstanding talents advance in great numbers, flourishing like luxuriant oak thickets—whether cut for firewood or piled up for sacrificial bonfires, none are unsuitable—so how could the roster of worthies possibly contain them all! Yet what your servant now worries about is not that the multitude of scholars are insufficient to fill the quota of those selected, but that once selected, they may not be suited for practical employment; not that the writings recorded here lack literary refinement, but that their literary refinement goes too far and departs from their substance. Why is this? Testing and receiving men on the basis of their words, though originating in the age of Shun of Yu, sought only those who were loyal and upright, fit to serve as the ruler's limbs and his ears and eyes. Later on, when the examination system arose, it likewise selected only those who understood the affairs of the present age and were versed in the arts of the former sages, for the purpose of employing them was inherently such as this. In the present age, the writing produced for the civil service examinations grows daily more extravagant…

title: 萬曆四年順天府鄉試錄
text:
麗至不可加矣而士猶馳騖
不止視先進渾厚爾雅之風
若非所屑然者曽弗知鼇帨
愈工本真愈遠蓋浸淫不已
而纖華竒僻襲諸子以緣飾
六經者種種有之豈
聖天子敦本尚實冀得真才意哉
===
夫龍興致雲鶴鳴子和言類
應也若
上以實下不免以文
上以醇下不免以雜
上以正下不免以僻則學術且背
而馳何敢應之足云故臣兹
校諸士之文罔敢苟同時好
alt_text:
麗至不可加矣而士猶馳騖
不止視先進渾厚爾雅之風
若非所屑然者曾弗知鞶帨
愈工本真愈遠蓋浸淫不已
而纖華奇僻襞諸子以緣飾
六經者種種有之豈
聖天子敦本尚實兾得真才意哉
===
夫龍興致雲鶴鳴子和言類
應也若
上以實下不免以文
上以醇下不免以雜
上以正下不免以僻則學術且背
而馳何敬應之足云故〔臣〕茲
校諸士之文罔敢苟同時好
punctuated: 麗，至不可加矣。而士猶馳騖不止，視先進渾厚爾雅之風，若非所屑然者，曽弗知鼇帨愈工，本真愈遠。蓋浸淫不已，而纖華竒僻，襲諸子以緣飾六經者，種種有之。豈聖天子敦本尚實，冀得真才意哉？夫龍興致雲，鶴鳴子和，言類應也。若上以實，下不免以文；上以醇，下不免以雜；上以正，下不免以僻，則學術且背而馳，何敢應之足云？故臣兹校諸士之文，罔敢苟同時好，
translation_en:
…ornate, to the point where nothing more can be added. Yet scholars still pursue this without cease, viewing the substantial, generous, and refined style of their predecessors as if it were beneath their notice. They utterly fail to realize that the more skillful the petty rhetorical embellishments [? 鼇帨, for 鞶帨], the further one strays from genuine substance. Indeed, as this trend spreads unabated, there are all manner of writings that are delicate, showy, strange, and eccentric, borrowing from the Various Masters to dress up the Six Classics. How could this be the intention of the Sacred Son of Heaven in emphasizing fundamentals, valuing substance, and hoping to obtain true talent?

Now, when the dragon rises it summons the clouds, and when the crane cries its young answer—this speaks of things responding to their own kind. If the Sovereign seeks substance while those below cannot avoid offering mere literary flourish; if the Sovereign seeks purity while those below cannot avoid offering a medley; if the Sovereign seeks orthodoxy while those below cannot avoid offering eccentricity—then scholarship will run in the very opposite direction, and how could one speak of any true response? Therefore, in examining the essays of the scholars on this occasion, your servant has not dared to casually conform to current fashions;…

title: 萬曆四年順天府鄉試錄
text:
必文質相扶中竅當物者取
之其根心切理質言無華者
亟取之諸騁逐于浮艷淄綴
于異說者雖工不錄蓋曰文
體關乎士習而人才視以汚
隆故寧去彼取此期得篤實
朴茂之士足爲縣官用也且
===
致用之本我
皇上幸學訓廸師生不已備乎曰
治平之道具在六經體驗推行
寔資化理士誠佩服
聖謨湛涵經旨存之心而温良醞
藉發之文而平正通達措之
躬而易直端方抒之業而光

必文質相扶中窾當物者取
之其根心切理質貫言無華者
亟取之諸騁逐于浮艷淄綴
于異說者雖工不錄蓋曰文
體關乎士習而人才視以汚
隆故寧去彼取此期得篤實
朴茂之士足爲縣官用也且
===
致用之本我
皇上幸學訓廸師生不已備乎曰
治平之道具在六經體驗推行
寔資化理士誠佩服
聖謨湛涵經旨存之心而温良醞
藉揆之文而平正通達措之
躬而易直端方抒之業而光
punctuated: 必文質相扶、中竅當物者取之，其根心切理、質言無華者亟取之；諸騁逐于浮艷、淄綴于異說者，雖工不錄。蓋曰文體關乎士習，而人才視以汚隆，故寧去彼取此，期得篤實朴茂之士，足爲縣官用也。且致用之本，我皇上幸學訓廸師生，不已備乎？曰「治平之道具在《六經》，體驗推行，寔資化理。」士誠佩服聖謨，湛涵經旨，存之心而温良醞藉，發之文而平正通達，措之躬而易直端方，抒之業而光
translation_en: …I selected only those essays in which refinement and substance supported one another, hitting the mark and fitting the subject; and I eagerly selected those rooted in the mind and close to principle, expressed in plain words without华飾 (ostentatious ornament). As for all those that chased after flashy elegance or were stained and patched together with heterodox doctrines, even if skilfully wrought, I did not admit them. For literary style is bound up with the habits of scholars, and the rise or decline of talent depends upon it; thus I would rather reject the latter and choose the former, hoping to obtain earnest, substantial, simple, and upright scholars who are fit to be of service to the state. Moreover, as for the foundation of practical service, did not Our Sovereign Emperor, when visiting the Imperial University to instruct and guide the teachers and students, already set it forth completely? He said: "The Way of governing and bringing peace to the world is entirely contained in the Six Classics; experiencing them personally and putting them into practice truly aids transformative governance." If scholars genuinely take to heart the Imperial counsels and immerse themselves deeply in the meaning of the Classics—preserving it in their minds so as to be gentle, good, and deeply cultivated; expressing it in their writing so as to be balanced, upright, and perspicacious; applying it in their personal conduct so as to be straightforward, honest, and square; and manifesting it in their achievements so as to be…

title: 萬曆四年順天府鄉試錄
text:
明俊偉即無論其近者雖虞
廷之九德俊乂必茲其選矣
國家其又何求顧因言考衷臣
可覘而知之自獻成信臣莫
愛而助之也諸士勗哉必也
言即可行學即可用平居以
爲準的而在事若操左券是
===
謂
聖世真才其于感遇論報可無負
矣得士若此臣亦何患焉有
如不然而本末相戾初終頓
殊是不惓于言者乃浮于行
先資之具徒弁髦耳此直硜
硜者不爲矧

國家其又何求顧因言考衷臣
可覘而知之自獻成信臣莫
愛而助之也諸士勗哉必也
言即可行學即可用平居以
為準的而在事若操左券是
===
謂
聖世真才其于感遇論報可無負
矣得士若此臣亦何患焉有
如不然而本末相戾初終頓
殊是不浮于言者乃浮于行
先資之具徒弁髦耳此直逕
逕者不為矧
punctuated: 明俊偉，即無論其近者，雖虞廷之九德俊乂，必茲其選矣，國家其又何求？顧因言考衷，臣可覘而知之；自獻成信，臣莫愛而助之也。諸士勗哉！必也言即可行，學即可用，平居以爲準的，而在事若操左券，是謂聖世真才，其于感遇論報，可無負矣。得士若此，臣亦何患焉？有如不然，而本末相戾，初終頓殊，是不惓于言者，乃浮于行，先資之具，徒弁髦耳。此直硜硜者不爲，矧
translation_en: …illustrious and magnificent—not to speak of those of recent times, even the eminent worthies possessing the Nine Virtues at the court of Yu [Shun] must surely be selected from among such men; what more could the state seek? Yet while examining their inner hearts through their words is something I, Your Majesty's servant, can observe and know, offering themselves in fulfilled trustworthiness is something in which, however much I cherish them, I cannot assist them. May the scholars exert themselves! Only when what they say can immediately be put into practice, and what they learn can immediately be put to use—taking this as their standard in ordinary life, and holding it like the left half of a tally when engaged in public affairs—can they be called true talents of a sagely age, who will not have failed in appreciating their fortunate encounter and repaying their debt of gratitude. In obtaining scholars such as these, what worry would I, Your Majesty's servant, have? If it is not so, and root and branch contradict each other while beginning and end suddenly diverge, then those who are untiring in their words will turn out to be superficial in their deeds, and the essays by which they first presented themselves will merely be cast aside like a boyhood cap. Even a stubbornly petty man would not act thus; how much less…

title: 萬曆四年順天府鄉試錄
text:
堯舜在上觀光用賓濟濟藹藹以
興者乃爲是歟即進而揚于
大廷又何以追儷于帝臣之敬
應者歟詩曰彼都人士出言
有章行歸于周萬民所望夫
都人士固萬民之望也惟不
第出言有章而以行之周者
===
副之將建首善以率先天下
寔自茲始
聖天子觀文化成之盛直揖唐虞
于千載之上可也若是則多
士匪徒用以報且足以風矣
於乎尚重圖之哉
承直郎右春坊右中允兼翰
alt_text:
堯舜在上觀光用賓濟濟藹藹以
興者乃爲是歟即進而揚于
大廷又何以追儷于帝臣之欽
應者歟詩曰彼都人士出言
有章行歸于周萬民所望夫
都人士固萬民之望也惟不
第出言有章而以行之周者
副之將建首善以率先天下
寔自茲始
===
聖天子觀文化成之盛直揖唐虞
于千載之上可也若是則多
士匪徒用以報且足以風矣
於乎尚重圖之哉
承直郎右春坊右中允兼翰
punctuated:
堯舜在上，觀光用賓，濟濟藹藹以興者，乃爲是歟？即進而揚于大廷，又何以追儷于帝臣之敬應者歟？《詩》曰：「彼都人士，出言有章，行歸于周，萬民所望。」夫都人士，固萬民之望也。惟不第出言有章，而以行之周者副之，將建首善以率先天下，寔自茲始。聖天子觀文化成之盛，直揖唐、虞于千載之上可也。若是，則多士匪徒用以報，且足以風矣。於乎！尚重圖之哉。
承直郎、右春坊右中允兼翰
translation_en:
… when a ruler like Yao and Shun is on high, would those who rise in dignified and harmonious multitude to behold the glory of the realm and be received as guests of the king act in such a way? And even if they should advance and be presented at the Great Court, how could they ever rival the reverent responsiveness of the ministers of the ancient sage-emperors? The Book of Odes (Shijing) says: "Those men of the capital, / In their speech they have elegance; / Their conduct returns to faithfulness and integrity, / And the myriad people look up to them." Indeed, the men of the capital are naturally those to whom the myriad people look up. Only when they not merely display elegance in their speech, but also match it with faithfulness and integrity in their conduct, will the establishment of the highest model of goodness to lead the entire realm truly begin from this. Then the flourishing of our Sacred Son of Heaven in observing cultural patterns to transform and perfect the world may directly salute the eras of Tang and Yu across a thousand years! If it be thus, then the many scholars will not merely use this to repay the throne, but will also suffice to inspire the realm by their example. Alas! May they earnestly take heed of this!

Gentleman for Fostering Uprightness, Companion of the Right in the Right Secretariat of the Heir Apparent, concurrently Han…

辭也者，各指其所之。

昔者聖人之作《易》也，將以順性命之理，是以立天之道曰陰與陽，立地之道曰柔與剛，立人之道曰仁與義。兼三才而兩之，故《易》六畫而成卦；分陰分陽，迭用柔

The Master is good at leading one on step by step. He broadens me with learning and restrains me with ritual, so that even if I wanted to stop, I could not. Having exhausted all my ability, there seems to be something standing lofty before me; though I wish to follow it, there is no way to do so.

Sincerity is self-completion, and the Way is self-direction. Sincerity is the beginning and end of things; without sincerity there would be nothing. Therefore, the noble man regards the attainment of sincerity as most precious.

Confucius said: "Hold it fast, and it remains; let it go, and it is lost. Its going out and coming in have no fixed time, and no one knows its abode—is it not the mind of which this is said?"

Six at the beginning: With sincerity, cleaving to it brings no blame. When there is sincerity filling an earthen vessel, in the end other good fortune will come.

The Commentary on the Images (Xiang) says: The marsh rises above the earth—Gathering Together (Cui). Thus the noble man repairs his weapons of war in order to guard against the unforeseen.

The appended phrases each indicate where the line is going.

精研妙契獨邁前聞且明示學二帝三王之意
揭諸
殿廷
手疏十二事之警置諸
===
座右淵淵乎帝王
祖宗之心法舉遠示而近述之矣謂學得其要
非歟諸生蹤不登
王庭然衣被
末光計必有得於傳聞者誠思殫其生平之
蘊不識進此而有裨於
聖修者否願具言之毋讓
問自昔言治不曰視諸故府則曰奉行故
□□其敝也則曰去其籍蓋籍之重如此
punctuated:
天子冲聖，日披經訓，陳圖史而講明之，至理奧義，自得為多。故或因論政而發明經旨，或因論史而商諏治道；至如《丹扆》、《大寶》諸箴，悉付訓詁，而精研妙契，獨邁前聞。且明示學二帝三王之意，揭諸殿廷；手疏十二事之警，置諸座右。淵淵乎！帝王、祖宗之心法，舉遠宗而近述之矣，謂學得其要非歟？諸生雖不登王庭，然衣被末光，計必有得於傳聞者。誠思殫其生平之蘊，不識進此而有裨於聖修者否？願具言之，毋讓。
問：自昔言治，不曰「視諸故府」，則曰「奉行故□」；□敝也，則曰「去其籍」。蓋籍之重如此。
translation_en:
… [Now] the Son of Heaven, in his youthful sageliness, daily opens the teachings of the Classics, setting out charts and histories to lecture upon and elucidate them; of their ultimate principles and profound meanings, much has been grasped through his own personal realization. Thus he sometimes elucidates the purport of the Classics in connection with discussing governance, and sometimes deliberates upon the Way of rule in connection with discussing history. Even such admonitions as the Admonitions on the Vermilion Screen (Danyi zhen) and the Admonitions on the Great Treasure (Dabao zhen) have all been consigned to exegesis, while his refined investigation and wondrous comprehension uniquely surpass what was heard in former times. Moreover, he has clearly manifested his intent to emulate the Two Emperors and Three Kings, displaying it in the palace halls; and with his own hand he has written out twelve admonitory items, placing them to the right of his throne. How profound! The method of the mind-and-heart of the ancient emperors and kings and of the Imperial Ancestors—all of it he reveres from afar and transmits near at hand. May it not be said that his learning has grasped the essential? Although you students have not ascended to the royal court, you are bathed in the furthest reaches of his radiance, and we reckon there must be things you have learned by report. If you truly think to exhaust the store of your lifelong learning, we do not know whether there is anything you might offer beyond this that could be of benefit to the Emperor's sagely self-cultivation? Pray state it in full, and do not hold back.

Question: Since antiquity, those who have spoken of governance have said either "inspect what is in the old repositories" or "carry out established [precedents]" [?]; and when [governance] fell into decay, it was said that "they did away with the records." Such, indeed, is the importance of official records! …

title: 萬曆四年順天府鄉試錄
text:
國家之制無論巨細非奉
令甲不得輒有所請雖跅弛不𮖐之士且循
途守轍不敢少踰寸尺倉卒不意之事
亦旁引遐據無得輒用便宜何者籍具
故也今所籍爲故事而藏之故府者非
大明會典乎會典本諸司職掌
高皇帝所創定
列聖相承因革損益代有不同
敬皇帝始命儒臣裒集成書頒布天下自弘治
===
壬戌迄今六十餘年未接其後事美聖嘉
靖中曾一續修書成而未頒也
天子加惠臣民特下
明詔命輔臣開局編摩載筆伊始而義例未
定也在弘治初儒臣蓋欲倣唐六典議
既中格然唐孰與周周亦有六典今所
當倣者果安在歟或以爲周唐建官不
同而
會典實本周官之舊第宜仍其舊編益以新

壬戌迄今六十餘年未接其後事蓋嘉
靖中曾一續修書成而未頒也
===
天子加惠臣民特下
明詔命輔臣開局編摩載筆伊始而義例未
定也在弘治初儒臣蓋欲倣唐六典議
既中格然唐孰與周周亦有六典今所
當倣者果安在歟或以爲周唐建官不
同而
會典實本周官之舊第宜仍其舊編益以新
punctuated: 國家之制，無論巨細，非奉令甲，不得輒有所請。雖跅弛不𮖐之士，且循途守轍，不敢少踰寸尺；倉卒不意之事，亦旁引遐據，無得輒用便宜。何者？籍具故也。今所籍爲故事而藏之故府者，非《大明會典》乎？《會典》本《諸司職掌》，高皇帝所創定，列聖相承，因革損益，代有不同。敬皇帝始命儒臣裒集成書，頒布天下。自弘治壬戌迄今六十餘年，未接其後事。美聖[？]嘉靖中曾一續修，書成而未頒也。天子加惠臣民，特下明詔，命輔臣開局編摩，載筆伊始，而義例未定也。在弘治初，儒臣蓋欲倣《唐六典》，議既中格。然唐孰與周？周亦有六典，今所當倣者，果安在歟？或以爲周、唐建官不同，而《會典》實本《周官》之舊，第宜仍其舊編，益以新
translation_en: In the institutions of the dynasty, regardless of whether a matter is great or small, unless one acts in accordance with the primary statutes (lingjia), one may not arbitrarily submit a request. Even unrestrained and untamed scholars follow the established path and keep to the tracks, not daring to overstep by even an inch or a foot; in sudden and unexpected matters, officials likewise cite analogous and distant precedents, and are not permitted to act at their own discretion. Why is this? Because the statutory records are complete. Now, is not that which is recorded as precedent and stored in the archives the Collected Statutes of the Great Ming (Da Ming huidian)? The Collected Statutes is based on the Functions of the Various Offices (Zhusi zhizhang), which was originally established by Emperor Gao [the Hongwu Emperor]. As successive sage emperors inherited the throne, continuities and changes, additions and reductions differed from reign to reign. Emperor Jing [the Hongzhi Emperor] first commanded Confucian officials to compile these into a book and promulgate it throughout the realm. From the renxu year of the Hongzhi era [1502] to the present is more than sixty years, and subsequent matters have not been appended to it. During the [xian? / former Emperor's?] [?] Jiajing era, a continuation was once compiled, but though the book was completed, it was never promulgated. The Son of Heaven, bestowing favor upon his officials and people, has specially issued an explicit edict commanding the Grand Secretaries to open a bureau to compile and edit it. The work of recording has just begun, yet the editorial principles and guidelines have not been settled. At the beginning of the Hongzhi era, the Confucian officials had wished to model it on the Six Statutes of the Tang (Tang liudian), but the proposal was shelved midway. Yet how does the Tang compare with the Zhou? The Zhou also had its six statutes; where, indeed, does the model we ought to follow today lie? Some hold that the establishment of offices in the Zhou and the Tang was different, and that the Collected Statutes is in fact based on the old system of the Offices of Zhou (Zhouguan), so we should simply retain its old arrangement and add the new…

title: 萬曆四年順天府鄉試錄
text:
事不知是編也果與周唐之典同乎否
歟抑或有當更定而可以補義例之所
不及者歟夫明於先聖之術者必習於
當世之務書稱成憲詩詠舊章其來尚
矣法果一成而不可變安用續編誠可
變通自今數十年後將復猶今之視昔
是書何為只何成憲舊章之云也主司
亦與載筆之列者願聞其說
問天下無不可為之事所貴有任事之人
===
===
夫任事之人豈易得哉得之或未易知
知之未必盡其用用之又或議其後令
在事者指以為戒此任事之人所以愈
不易得也試借前事籌之夫受命備邊
不能使虜不敢入比入乃反禁捕虜者
數入數收保民得無擾乎何以明非怯
也市租輸幕府日饗不用之士何以明
非費也既數歲甫一接戰尚未當虜輒
以數千人委焉何以明非敗也羌虜初

translation_en:
…matters. Yet one wonders whether this compilation is indeed identical with the canons of the Zhou and the Tang or not? Or are there perhaps parts that ought to be revised so as to supply what the editorial principles have failed to cover? Now, those who understand the arts of the Former Sages are necessarily versed in the affairs of the present age. The Book of Documents praises the "established constitutions" and the Book of Odes sings of the "old statutes"—their origins go back to antiquity. If laws, once established, were truly immutable, what need would there be for a supplementary compilation? Yet if they can truly be adapted to change, then several decades from now people will again look upon the present just as the present looks upon the past; what then would be the purpose of this book, and how could one speak of [? "只何"] "established constitutions" and "old statutes"? As Examiner, I too am among those charged with wielding the brush on this project, and I wish to hear your views.

Question: Under heaven there is no affair that cannot be accomplished; what is valued is having men who will take responsibility for affairs. Yet how could men who take responsibility for affairs be easy to obtain? Even when they are obtained, they are not easily recognized; when recognized, they are not necessarily employed to the full; and when employed, critics may afterwards carp at them, causing those who are in charge of affairs to point to them as a warning. This is why men who take responsibility for affairs become ever harder to obtain. Let us borrow examples from past affairs to reckon this: Someone receives a commission to defend the frontier, yet cannot keep the northern raiders from daring to invade; and when they do invade, he instead forbids anyone to capture the raiders. As they repeatedly invade and he repeatedly gathers the populace into the fortifications for protection, can the people avoid being disturbed? How can it be shown that this was not cowardice? When the market taxes were all delivered to his military headquarters and he daily feasted troops who were not sent into action, how can it be shown that this was not wastefulness? After several years, when he finally engaged in battle once, before even meeting the main force of the raiders, he readily abandoned several thousand men to them; how can it be shown that this was not a defeat? title: 萬曆四年順天府鄉試錄
text:
動上固老之而問誰可將者旣自許無
踰老臣宜有定畫矣顧曰兵難隃度比
至馳上方畧第欲罷騎兵屯田夫因天
時誅不義宜可滅此而朝食璽書三問
廷議豈皆非□何堅持不顧也于時後
將軍但守破羌彊弩出擊計固兩用虜
所以破壤何以明皆留屯功也汴鎭擅
命久蕞爾一州發諸道兵窮四年之力
未得志焉舉朝爭言罷兵乃獨請督戰
===
當是時師老財匱矣何以明罷兵之非
計也北河數决欲南疏故道而尚書行
河自濟濮數十里井量高下岸測淺深
謂故道必不可復且山東歲侵而聚二
十萬眾于此恐爲他日憂蓋亦老成長
慮然則何以明役不大興害不能已也
由前二事畏事者將依托焉由後二事
喜事者將奔走焉當何任而可古有大
事必集眾議而後行彼皆違眾獨行其

translation_en:
… stirred, the Emperor indeed considered him too old and asked who could serve as general. Since he vouched for himself by saying, "None surpasses this old minister," he ought to have had a settled plan; yet he replied, "Military affairs are difficult to gauge from afar." When he arrived, he sent a courier to submit his strategic plan, which merely proposed dismissing the cavalry and establishing military agricultural colonies. Now, taking advantage of the opportune season of Heaven to punish the unrighteous, one ought to have been able to destroy them before breakfast. Imperial letters questioned him three times—could the court deliberations have been entirely wrong [?]? Why did he cling so stubbornly to his view without regard for them? At that time, the General of the Rear merely held a defensive posture while the General Who Smashes the Qiang and the General of Strong Crossbowmen went out to attack, so both strategies were in fact employed. As for why the caitiffs were broken and ruined [?], how can it be made clear that the credit belonged entirely to maintaining the agricultural colonies?

When the military command at Bian [Huai-Xi / Cai prefecture] had long usurped authority—a tiny single prefecture—troops from various circuits were mobilized and the strength of four years was exhausted without achieving success. The entire court vied in arguing to call off the campaign, yet one man alone requested to go oversee the fighting in person. At that time, the army was worn out and finances were depleted; how could it be made clear that calling off the troops was the wrong plan?

When the northern reaches of the Yellow River repeatedly breached its dikes, there was a desire to dredge the old southern channel. Yet when the Minister inspected the River across several dozen li from Ji and Pu, measuring the elevation by means of wells and sounding the depth along the banks, he maintained that the old channel definitely could not be restored; moreover, since Shandong was suffering from a year of dearth, gathering two hundred thousand men there would likely become a cause of worry for the future—which was indeed the far-sighted concern of a seasoned statesman. Yet how, then, could it be made clear that unless a grand corvée project was launched, the disaster could not be stopped?

Following the first two examples, those who shrink from action will find an excuse to hide behind; following the latter two examples, those who are overly eager for action will rush headlong into things. What sort of responsibility should one take for it to be right? In antiquity, when there were great affairs, one always gathered the deliberations of the multitude before acting. Those men all went against the multitude to carry out alone their own …

title: 萬曆四年順天府鄉試錄
text:
意議固可廢邪往昔所稱任事之臣其
事若此設以施於
今日人其謂何諸士行且進而在事各量所
自任以意對
問久任之法經見虞周治蓋倬哉盛矣至
於兩漢而效可睹也繇漢以來論者益
詳有諫守長數易者有論久任當行者
有言久任之效者有言不久任之弊者
竝宜見采於時而治效寢不逮古何歟
===
聖天子鑒古圖治
明詔有司力行久任以復虞周之軌
德意至盛顧人情狃於故習率已歎淹而選法
亦不能無壅此何以說也或謂先王之
世有超遷以拔茂異有考課以汰蠧蠢
故沉滯者有所振不肖者無所妨而久
任可常行無弊審如是則今之勞能表
卓者輒見登延而三歲大計網非疎也
乃紛紜之議猶以□□□□然則是終不

punctuated:
意，議固可廢邪？往昔所稱任事之臣，其事若此，設以施於今日，人其謂何？諸士行且進而在事，各量所自任，以意對。

問：久任之法，經見虞、周，治蓋倬哉盛矣！至於兩漢，而效可睹也。繇漢以來，論者益詳：有諫守長數易者，有論久任當行者，有言久任之效者，有言不久任之弊者。竝宜見采於時，而治效寢不逮古，何歟？聖天子鑒古圖治，明詔有司力行久任，以復虞、周之軌，德意至盛。顧人情狃於故習，率已歎淹，而選法亦不能無壅，此何以說也？或謂先王之世，有超遷以拔茂異，有考課以汰蠧蠢，故沉滯者有所振，不肖者無所妨，而久任可常行無弊。審如是，則今之勞能表卓者輒見登延，而三歲大計，網非疎也。乃紛紜之議，猶以□□□□。然則是終不
translation_en:
… own will; can public deliberation really be dispensed with? The actions of those who in the past were praised as ministers who took on responsibility were like this; suppose they were carried out today, what would people say? You gentlemen are about to advance into office and take up duties; let each of you measure what responsibility you would take upon yourself and reply with your thoughts.

Question: The method of long tenure in office is seen in the Classics for the Yu and Zhou eras, when governance was brilliantly flourishing! Coming down to the Former and Latter Han, its effectiveness can still be observed. From the Han onward, commentators have discussed it in ever greater detail: there were those who remonstrated against the frequent replacement of Grand Defenders and District Magistrates, those who argued that long tenure ought to be practiced, those who spoke of the efficacy of long tenure, and those who spoke of the abuses of not practicing long tenure. All of these views ought to have been adopted in their times, and yet the effectiveness of governance gradually failed to match antiquity—why is this?

Our Sacred Son of Heaven, taking antiquity as a mirror in planning for governance, has clearly诏 [decreed to] the authorities to vigorously implement long tenure in order to restore the model of Yu and Zhou; His virtuous intent is most abundant. Yet human sentiment, accustomed to old habits, generally already laments stagnation in office, while the system of official selection also cannot avoid congestion—how is this to be explained? Some say that in the age of the former kings, there were extraordinary promotions to select the outstanding and exceptional, and merit evaluations to weed out the corrupt and foolish; thus those bogged down in low positions had a means to be roused, the unworthy had no way to cause hindrance, and long tenure could be constantly practiced without abuse. If it is indeed so, then today those whose toil and ability stand out brilliantly are readily promoted and advanced, and in the triennial Great Reckoning the net is by no means wide-meshed. Yet clamorous discussions still take […4 illegible characters…]. This being so, is this ultimately not …

title: 萬曆四年順天府鄉試錄
text:
□□歟將行之不得其術歟抑已得其
術而紛紜之議不足卹歟夫虞周制莫
可詳乃史敘漢宣久任之美必以樞機
周密品式備具為稱又似有道以參伍
其間者豈今固未之講歟諸士茲且待
用於有司矣願極言之令經世者有所
決擇焉
問周禮惟王建國以為民極商頌邦畿千
里肇域四海久矣夫京師之重也
===
國家定鼎燕京北枕大漠前襟漕河左齊魯
右秦晉包舉伊洛湘漢轉餉江淮之間
旁引閩蜀南盡交廣滇粤輿圖一統前
世莫及今海内承平九州筐篚歲至
朝廷下咫尺之檄郡國長吏恐懼奔走無敢
後先豈不稱極治乎哉然有識之士每
為長慮請言其大者北虜已受約束而
薊門之戍歲費累未已也頃虜一小入
頗聞失利頻年練兵實效安在漕渠為

punctuated:
□□歟？將行之不得其術歟？抑已得其術，而紛紜之議不足卹歟？夫虞、周制莫可詳，乃史敘漢宣久任之美，必以樞機周密、品式備具為稱，又似有道以參伍其間者，豈今固未之講歟？諸士茲且待用於有司矣，願極言之，令經世者有所決擇焉。

問：《周禮》：「惟王建國，以為民極。」《商頌》：「邦畿千里，肇域四海。」久矣夫，京師之重也！國家定鼎燕京，北枕大漠，前襟漕河，左齊、魯，右秦、晉，包舉伊、洛、湘、漢，轉餉江、淮之間，旁引閩、蜀，南盡交、廣、滇、粤，輿圖一統，前世莫及。今海内承平，九州筐篚歲至，朝廷下咫尺之檄，郡國長吏恐懼奔走，無敢後先，豈不稱極治乎哉！然有識之士，每為長慮，請言其大者：北虜已受約束，而薊門之戍歲費累未已也。頃虜一小入，頗聞失利，頻年練兵，實效安在？漕渠為
translation_en:
… [can]not [be carried out?], or is it that in implementing it the proper method has not been found? Or is it that the proper method has already been found, and the clamorous discussions are not worth heeding? Now, the institutions of Yu [Shun] and the Zhou cannot be known in detail, yet when the histories recount the excellence of long tenure under Emperor Xuan of Han, they invariably praise the thoroughness of his central administrative mechanisms and the completeness of his regulations and standards. It seems there was also a way of cross-checking and coordinating things within the system—could it be that today we have simply not yet studied this? You gentlemen are now awaiting appointment by the authorities; I ask that you speak on this exhaustively, so that those who order the world may have a basis for making their choices.

Question: The Rites of Zhou (Zhouli) states: "It is the king who establishes the state, to serve as the standard for the people." The Hymns of Shang (Shangsong) says: "The royal domain of a thousand li initiates the boundaries of the four seas." Long indeed has been the importance of the capital! Our Dynasty established its capital at Yanjing [Beijing], resting against the great desert to the north andfronted by the Grand Canal like a lapel, with Qi and Lu to the left, Qin and Jin to the right, encompassing the Yi, Luo, Xiang, and Han rivers, transporting grain supplies from between the Yangtze and Huai rivers, drawing in Min [Fujian] and Shu [Sichuan] on the flanks, and reaching all the way south to Jiao [Jiaozhi], Guang [Guangdong and Guangxi], Dian [Yunnan], and Yue. The unification of the map is something no previous era has matched. Today all within the seas enjoys peace, tribute baskets from the Nine Provinces arrive every year, and when the Court sends down a brief dispatch, the chief officials of commanderies and principalities hasten in fear and trembling, none daring to lag or overstep—is this not what is called the ultimate good governance? Yet men of insight constantly take long-range thought; allow me to speak of the greatest concerns. The northern caitiffs have already submitted to treaty restraints, yet the annual expenditures for the garrisons at Jimen have accumulated without end. Recently, when the caitiffs made one small incursion, we heard considerable news of setbacks—where, then, is the practical effect of training troops year after year? As for the Grand Canal being…

title: 萬曆四年順天府鄉試錄
text:
梗議者以為不可治去而他圖蓋行河
者未至而東土騷然矣頃乃併力下流
頗聞報效然異時治河何嘗不報效歲
復如故而未睹其竟也百官六軍九邊
仰給於東南平居無事而民間皇皇若
不聊生以為不在民則在官而
國用非有餘以為加賦而常徵之外多所節
省又非有方二三千里水旱之災盜賊
之擾乃其故何也議者為根本至計以
===
為瀕海沃壤當募民田近郊輔郡當列
兵屯三營士馬當簡四方游惰當驅此
其策可施行否今欲使
京師無失其重舉天下運於指顧之中而聯
合為一體足以域四海為民極焉何施
而可諸士習于
都邑之故其各以所見聞著于篇

頗聞報效然異時治河何嘗不㮣效歲
復如故而未睹其竟也百官六軍九邊

===
爲瀕海沃壤當募民田近郊輔郡當列
兵屯三營士馬當簡四方游惰當驅此
其策可施行否今欲使
京師無失其重舉天下運於指顧之中而聯
合爲一體足以域四海爲民極焉何施
而可諸士習于
都邑之故其各以所見聞著于篇
punctuated: 梗，議者以為不可治，去而他圖，蓋行河者未至而東土騷然矣。頃乃併力下流，頗聞報效，然異時治河何嘗不報效，歲復如故，而未睹其竟也。百官、六軍、九邊仰給於東南，平居無事，而民間皇皇若不聊生。以為不在民則在官，而國用非有餘；以為加賦，而常徵之外多所節省；又非有方二三千里水旱之災、盜賊之擾，乃其故何也？議者為根本至計，以為瀕海沃壤當募民田，近郊輔郡當列兵屯，三營士馬當簡，四方游惰當驅，此其策可施行否？今欲使京師無失其重，舉天下運於指顧之中，而聯合為一體，足以域四海、為民極焉，何施而可？諸士習于都邑之故，其各以所見聞著于篇。
translation_en: …obstructed. Those who deliberate on the matter consider it impossible to repair, abandoning it to seek other plans; yet before those sent to inspect the waterways had even arrived, the eastern regions were already in turmoil. Recently, efforts have been concentrated on the lower reaches, and we have heard some reports of success. Yet in past times when the river was controlled, when were there not reports of success? Still, year after year it reverts to its former state, and we have yet to see a final resolution. The hundred officials, the Six Armies, and the Nine Frontier Commands all depend on the Southeast for their supplies. In ordinary times of peace, the common people are nevertheless anxious and distressed as though they have no means of livelihood. If one supposes that wealth not with the people must be with the state, yet state finances have no surplus; if one supposes it is due to increased taxes, yet beyond the regular levies much has been economized and remitted; nor have there been floods, droughts, or bandit disturbances spanning two or three thousand li—what, then, is the reason for this? Those who deliberate on fundamental and supreme plans argue that people should be recruited to cultivate the fertile lands along the coast, military agricultural colonies should be arrayed in the suburban and metropolitan prefectures, the troops and horses of the Three Great Training Divisions should be culled and selected, and vagrant idlers from all quarters should be driven out—can these policies be put into practice or not? Now, if we wish to ensure that the Capital does not lose its weighty preeminence, so that the entire realm may be directed at the point of a finger and the turn of a gaze, united into a single body sufficient to encompass the Four Seas and serve as the standard for the people, what measures should be taken to achieve this? You scholars are well versed in the affairs of the capital; let each of you set forth in your essay what you have seen and heard.

title: 萬曆四年順天府鄉試錄
text:
第壹塲
四書
夫子循循然善誘人博我以文約我以禮
欲罷不能既竭吾才如有所立卓爾雖
欲從之末由也已
林雲龍
同考試官教諭姚批簡古周詳純雅明鬯
闡揚顏子心得聖道殆盡
同考試官教諭王批融會大意洗刷浮詞
邃養士也
同考試官學正郝批欲從末由正顏子造道
之深處是作獨得此意起束處尤超脫可錄
同考試官學正陳批塲中率以欲從末由
作復歎其難不知此正顏子之有得處是篇明徹典雅足
破陋說宜式多士
考試官右贊善許批卓爾末由本博約切近言
之得肯
考試官右中允何批得顏子歸功聖人意

第壹場

同考試官教諭姚　批　簡古周詳純雅明暢

闡揚顏子心得聖道殆盡

之深處是作獨得此意起束處尤超脫可錄
遂養士也
同考試官學正陳　批　場中率以欲從末由
作復歎其難不知此正顏子之有得處是篇明徹典雅足
破陋說宜式多士
考試官右贊善許　批　卓爾末由本博約切近言
之得肯
考試官右中允何　批　得顏子歸功聖人意
punctuated:
第壹塲
四書
「夫子循循然善誘人，博我以文，約我以禮，欲罷不能。既竭吾才，如有所立卓爾。雖欲從之，末由也已。」
林雲龍
同考試官教諭姚批：簡古周詳，純雅明鬯，闡揚顏子心得聖道殆盡。
同考試官教諭王批：融會大意，洗刷浮詞，邃養士也。
同考試官學正郝批：欲從末由，正顏子造道之深處，是作獨得此意。起束處尤超脫，可錄。
同考試官學正陳批：塲中率以「欲從末由」作復歎其難，不知此正顏子之有得處。是篇明徹典雅，足破陋說，宜式多士。
考試官右贊善許批：卓爾末由，本博約切近，言之得肯。
考試官右中允何批：得顏子歸功聖人意。
translation_en:
First Session
The Four Books
"The Master is good at leading one on step by step. He broadens me with culture and restrains me with ritual. Even if I wanted to stop, I could not. Having exhausted my abilities, there seems to be something standing lofty before me; though I wish to follow it, there is no way to do so." (Analects 9.11)
By Lin Yunlong 林雲龍
Associate Examiner and Instructor Yao 姚 comments: Concise, antique, thorough, and detailed; pure, elegant, clear, and fluent. It brings out almost completely what Yanzi 顏子 grasped in his heart of the Sage's Way.
Associate Examiner and Instructor Wang 王 comments: It thoroughly synthesizes the main meaning and washes away superficial verbiage. He is a scholar of profound cultivation.
Associate Examiner and Subprefectural Director of Studies Hao 郝 comments: "Wishing to follow it, yet having no way to do so" is precisely the deepest point of Yanzi's attainment in the Way. This composition alone grasps this meaning. Its opening and closing sections are especially transcendent; it is worthy of selection.
Associate Examiner and Subprefectural Director of Studies Chen 陳 comments: In the examination hall, candidates generally treated "wishing to follow it, yet having no way to do so" as a renewed sigh over its difficulty, not realizing that this is precisely where Yanzi achieved his realization. This essay is lucid, penetrating, and classically elegant—sufficient to dispel vulgar interpretations and fitting to serve as a model for the many scholars.
Examiner and Right Admonisher Xu 許 comments: What stands "lofty" with "no way to follow" is rooted in the immediate practice of broadening with culture and restraining with ritual; his discussion hits the mark.
Examiner and Right Companion He 何 comments: It captures Yanzi's intention of attributing the credit to the Sage.

title: 萬曆四年順天府鄉試錄
text:
大賢嘆聖教之善因以進聖道之深焉夫道可
以心遇不可以力從也顏子由博約而進乎此
其自得者深乎想其歸功聖人意謂始吾求道
於高堅前後之間志固欲速其化也既無得於
仰鑽瞻忽之際功未始不苦其難也幸而有夫
子之善誘焉循循然施之不拂其序而進之必
順其安慮回之寡陋無以盡道之變也先博我
以文凡所以開廣其見聞者燦然在吾心而禮
於是有餘資矣慮回之汗漫無以會道之歸也
===
復約我以禮凡所以檢制其行事者秩然在吾
心而文於是有實踐矣夫然後覺持循之有賴
而鼓吾樂進之心語嚮往之無窮而畢吾從事
之力彌高彌堅者因文禮以露其天真凝然若
與我俱立非仰鑽之徒勤矣在前在後者隨博
約而著於日用卓然若與我相參非瞻忽之靡
定矣蓋愈進也則愈親也使身或可即庶幾吾
志之竟成耳但可望也不可至也乃力無所庸
一如吾才之既竭何要之欲罷不能之初循夫

The great worthy sighed in admiration at the excellence of the Sage’s teaching, through which he advanced into the profundity of the Sage’s Way. Now, the Way can be met with the mind, but cannot be pursued by mere force. Master Yan (Yan Hui 顏回) advanced to this point by means of broadening with literature and restraining with ritual—how deep was his personal realization! Imagine how, in attributing the credit to the Sage, his thought was as follows: 

At first, when I sought the Way amid what seemed lofty, firm, before, and behind, my ambition was certainly to hasten its transformation; yet having gained nothing while looking up, boring in, gazing before, and suddenly finding it behind, in my efforts I never ceased to suffer from its difficulty. Fortunately, there was the Master’s skillful leading, whereby step by step he imparted it without violating its proper sequence, and advanced me always in accordance with what was natural and secure. 

Lest I, Hui, in my narrowness and ignorance, should have no means to exhaust the transformations of the Way, he first broadened me with literature; all that served to widen my experience and knowledge shone brightly in my mind, and ritual thereby had abundant resources to draw upon. Lest I, Hui, in my diffuseness and lack of focus, should have no means to grasp the ultimate convergence of the Way, he then restrained me with ritual; all that served to regulate and govern my conduct was ordered in my mind, and literature thereby found actual practice. 

Only then did I realize that I had something reliable to hold to and follow, which roused my heart to delight in advancing; and speaking of an endless aspiration, I exhausted my strength in pursuing the task. That which was ever loftier and ever firmer revealed its natural truth through literature and ritual, standing solidly as if right alongside me—it was no longer the futile toil of merely looking up and boring in! That which was in front and behind became manifest in daily use following upon broadening and restraining, standing out toweringly as if face to face with me—it was no longer the unsettled shifting of gazing before and suddenly seeing it behind! 

Indeed, the further I advanced, the closer it became. Had it been something my person could actually reach, perhaps my ambition might have been finally fulfilled! Yet it could only be gazed at from afar, and could not be arrived at; where physical effort was of no avail, it was just as when my talents had already been exhausted—what more could be done! In short, at the beginning, when I wished to stop but could not, I followed the Master’s…

… the Master's teaching in order to enter into it; and after finding that though I wished to follow it there was no way to do so, I held fast to the Master's teaching in order to await it. This is why I, Hui, never forget his skillful leading on. Looking at this, the depth of his attainment in the Way can thus be seen. Generally speaking, if one seeks the Way in the sage, then looking up at it, boring into it, gazing before and suddenly seeing it behind will not be enough; if one seeks the Way within oneself, then broadening oneself with learning and restraining oneself with ritual will be more than sufficient. Yet the teaching of broad learning and restraint by ritual was heard in common by all the disciples, whereas Master Yan alone exhausted his talent in it—for he surely knew that the Way lies within oneself [?]. Alas! Even the transmission of "refinement and singleness" at the court of Yu—how could it change this? Therefore it is said: "He brought forth the hidden store of the Sage, teaching ten thousand generations without end."

title: 萬曆四年順天府鄉試錄
text:
之所貴矣且天之生物也命之斯爲誠而率之
斯爲道一而已矣誠之言成也實心在我乃天
命之本然由與知與能而察于上下性何以全
形何以踐理固各足非有假於外也故曰自成
而道之本立矣道之言導也實理在物乃率性
之當然由達德達道以施于政治擇孰與明守
孰與固分亦各正非可諉於人也故曰自道而
誠之用行矣盍反其本觀之理得而聚於有物
非自始誠爲之始也理盡而歸於無物非自終
===
誠爲之終也誠旣與物爲終始則物亦與誠爲
有無苟焉不誠是爲無物矣故人心一有不實
則所爲皆妄也君子思以成身敢自棄乎實心
一或不存雖有爲亦虚也君子將以凝道容自
已乎致曲以至於能化賢之所以希聖者此也
盡性以至於如神聖之所以希天者此也是以
君子貴誠也能誠則終始萬物之理在我乃爲
有以自成而道亦行乎其中矣嗟乎此天德也
二帝三王之治皆由此出故當其時中和在上

punctuated: 之所貴矣。且天之生物也，命之斯爲誠，而率之斯爲道，一而已矣。誠之言成也，實心在我，乃天命之本然。由與知與能，而察于上下，性何以全？形何以踐？理固各足，非有假於外也。故曰「自成」，而道之本立矣。道之言導也，實理在物，乃率性之當然。由達德達道，以施于政治，擇孰與明？守孰與固？分亦各正，非可諉於人也。故曰「自道」，而誠之用行矣。盍反其本觀之？理得而聚於有，物非自始，誠爲之始也；理盡而歸於無，物非自終，誠爲之終也。誠旣與物爲終始，則物亦與誠爲有無；苟焉不誠，是爲無物矣。故人心一有不實，則所爲皆妄也，君子思以成身，敢自棄乎？實心一或不存，雖有爲亦虚也，君子將以凝道，容自已乎？致曲以至於能化，賢之所以希聖者此也；盡性以至於如神，聖之所以希天者此也。是以君子貴誠也。能誠，則終始萬物之理在我，乃爲有以自成，而道亦行乎其中矣。嗟乎！此天德也，二帝三王之治皆由此出。故當其時，中和在上，
translation_en:
… what [the noble man] values. Moreover, when Heaven gives birth to things, what it ordains in them is sincerity, and following this is the Way; they are one and the same.

"Sincerity" (cheng 誠) means "completion" (cheng 成). When a genuine heart-mind is within me, that is the original state of Heaven's mandate. From what even the simple can know and practice to what is discernible above and below—how is one's nature fulfilled? How is one's bodily form realized in conduct? The principle in each case is inherently sufficient in itself, without borrowing anything from outside. Thus it is said that sincerity "completes the self," and the foundation of the Way is established.

"The Way" (dao 道) means "to guide" (dao 導). When genuine principle inheres in affairs and things, that is the proper course of following one's nature. From the universal virtues and universal ways to their application in governance—who will choose them with clarity? Who will hold fast to them with firmness? Each person's allotted duty is likewise properly his own, not something that can be shifted onto others. Thus it is said that the Way "is what one must pursue oneself," and the function of sincerity is put into practice.

Why not return to its root and examine it? When principle is attained and gathers into being, a thing does not begin of itself; sincerity is what makes its beginning. When principle is exhausted and returns to non-being, a thing does not end of itself; sincerity is what makes its end. Since sincerity constitutes the end and beginning of things, things likewise depend on sincerity for their existence or non-existence; if there is any lack of sincerity, there is nothing at all. Therefore, once the human heart-mind has the slightest falsity, everything it does is vain; when the noble man seeks to complete his person, how dare he abandon himself? And if a genuine heart-mind should even for a moment fail to be preserved, though one takes action it is still empty; when the noble man seeks to consolidate the Way, how can he permit himself to cease?

Pushing partial goodness to its utmost until one can transform—this is whereby the worthy aspires to the sage. Developing one's nature to the utmost until one is like a spirit—this is whereby the sage aspires to Heaven. For this reason, the noble man values sincerity. When one is able to be sincere, the principle that ends and begins the myriad things resides within oneself; thus one has the means to complete oneself, and the Way is also practiced therein.

Alas! This is heavenly virtue, from which the governance of the Two Emperors and Three Kings all emerged. Thus in their times, equilibrium and harmony prevailed above, …

…Heaven and Earth and the myriad things each attained their proper place. For sincerity does not merely complete the self alone; the Way is shared as the Way with all under Heaven. Otherwise, even uniting the lords nine times and rectifying the realm as one would still amount to nothingness. How should one who seeks to attain sincerity proceed? I say: the key lies in vigilance over oneself when alone.

"Confucius said: 'Hold it fast, and it remains; let it go, and it perishes. Its going out and coming in have no fixed time, and no one knows its abode—surely this refers to the mind!'"
By Zhang Yusun 張育孫.

Associate Examiner Instructor Li 李 comments: In expounding the numinous intelligence of the mind, this composition possesses a singular flavor and ought to be recorded as a model.
Examiner Right Admonisher Xu 許 comments: The words are not prodigal, yet the meaning leaps vibrantly forth.
Examiner Right Companion He 何 comments: Intimate, pertinent, and full of flavor.

By observing how the Sage discussed the mind, one may know that the mind ought to be nourished. Extreme indeed is the unfathomable numinous intelligence of the mind! Its preservation or loss, its going out or coming in, have no fixed certainty, depending solely upon whether it is held fast or let go; from this the gentleman may know how to nourish it. Of old, Mencius discussed the human mind by analogy with the trees on Ox Mountain. Having already stated that nourishment has its successes and failures, and that growth and decay follow accordingly, he further cited the words of Confucius to serve as a warning. It is as if to say: Among the things in the world, there are indeed those which, even if held fast, do not necessarily…

text:
□者矣今則是惟無操一或操之即斂而存不
待持之久而始得也亦有舍之未必亡者矣今
則是惟無舍一或舍之即逸而亡不待放之久
而始失也方其存也吾見其時入矣未幾而復
亡焉入者未始不出也何定時乎方其入也吾
知其在內矣未幾而復出焉內者未始不外也
何定鄉乎若此者謂何惟心而已蓋凡物皆以
形用故滯於一定而不化乃心獨以神用故妙
於萬變而不居其體則大而動靜每乘乎氣機

There are also things that, when let go, are not necessarily lost; yet with this, it is only if one does not let go of it—for the moment one lets go of it, it escapes and is lost, without waiting to be abandoned for a long time before it is gone. Just when it is preserved, we see it enter at that moment, yet before long it is lost again; what has entered never fails to go out—what fixed time does it have? Just when it enters, we know it is within, yet before long it goes out again; what is within never fails to go outside—what fixed abode does it have? What is it that is like this? Could it be anything other than the mind? Indeed, all other things function through physical form, and so they are bogged down in a fixed state and do not transform; the mind alone functions through spirit, and so it operates wondrously across ten thousand changes without dwelling in one place. Its substance is great, yet its movement and stillness always ride upon the mechanisms of vital energy (qi); that which is subtle and hard to make manifest and that which is precarious and hard to make secure contend with one another for dominance—therefore at times it is preserved and at times it is lost. Such is the mind in man: gaining or losing it is very easy, while safeguarding and keeping it is very difficult. How could one fail to nourish it even for an instant! title: 萬曆四年順天府鄉試錄
text:
六居比之初謂始進之途君子最重也故方行
義惟知忠信爲質而已不敢雜以智術之私二
心之懷人臣大戒也故甫服官惟知无妄以往
而已不敢萌乎寵利之念此則精白以承休德
上不欺吾君也悃愊以施實惠下不罔吾民也
何咎之有然是孚也可以自責而不可以自恕
者也又必由內及外擴而充之慥慥乎无一毫
之虛假自始至終推而極之肫肫然无一息之
間斷如缶之盈乎物而无餘受焉將見誠之至
===
也難諶如天地且動矣矧顯比之聖有不倚毗
者乎爲臣而能獲乎上其吉也蓋有欲違弗克
者矣信之篤也无知如豚魚且感矣矧順從之
民有不悅服者乎居上而能治乎下其吉也蓋
有匪虞所思者矣吁初之有孚求寡過焉爾不
敢不勉也終之盈缶知自盡焉爾非有所覬也
然而无咎他吉乃理之自致焉君子所以誠之
爲貴歟雖然有孚之義豈但從政當如是哉漆
雕氏蓋言之矣吾斯之未能信古之人有先資

punctuated: 六居比之初，謂始進之途，君子最重也。故方行義，惟知忠信爲質而已，不敢雜以智術之私。二心之懷，人臣大戒也。故甫服官，惟知无妄以往而已，不敢萌乎寵利之念。此則精白以承休德，上不欺吾君也；悃愊以施實惠，下不罔吾民也，何咎之有？然是孚也，可以自責而不可以自恕者也。又必由內及外，擴而充之，慥慥乎无一毫之虛假；自始至終，推而極之，肫肫然无一息之間斷，如缶之盈乎物而无餘受焉。將見誠之至也，難諶如天地且動矣，矧顯比之聖有不倚毗者乎？爲臣而能獲乎上，其吉也，蓋有欲違弗克者矣。信之篤也，无知如豚魚且感矣，矧順從之民有不悅服者乎？居上而能治乎下，其吉也，蓋有匪虞所思者矣。吁！初之有孚，求寡過焉爾，不敢不勉也；終之盈缶，知自盡焉爾，非有所覬也。然而无咎、他吉，乃理之自致焉，君子所以誠之爲貴歟！雖然，有孚之義，豈但從政當如是哉？漆雕氏蓋言之矣：「吾斯之未能信。」古之人有先資…
translation_en:
As a yielding line (six) occupying the initial position of the hexagram Bi (Holding Together), this speaks of the path of first entering office, which the superior man regards as of the utmost importance. Therefore, when just beginning to practice righteousness, he knows only to take loyalty and trustworthiness as his substance, not daring to adulterate it with the selfishness of clever schemes. Harboring a divided heart is the great warning for a minister. Therefore, upon first assuming office, he knows only to go forward without falsehood, not daring to sprout thoughts of favor and profit. Thus, with pure integrity he upholds the sovereign's excellence and virtue, above not deceiving his ruler; with sincere devotion he bestows real benefits, below not deluding his people—what blame could there be?

Yet this sincerity (fu) is something with which one may hold oneself to account, not something with which one may excuse oneself. One must further expand and fill it out from within to without, earnestly allowing not a hair's breadth of falsity; and push it to the utmost from beginning to end, genuinely allowing not a single breath's interruption—just like an earthen jar (fou) filled with things until it can hold no more. Then one will see that when sincerity reaches its utmost, even Heaven and Earth, inscrutable as they are, will be moved—how much more will the sage of manifest union (xian bi) not rely upon and be aided by him? Being a minister and able to win the confidence of his superior, such good fortune is something that could not be turned away even if one wished to. When trustworthiness is deep, even creatures as ignorant as suckling pigs and fishes are moved—how much more will the compliant people not gladly submit? Occupying a position above and being able to govern those below, such good fortune comes in ways beyond what one could have anticipated in thought.

Alas! Possessing sincerity at the beginning is merely seeking to make few one's faults; one dares not fail to exert oneself. Filling the earthen jar in the end is merely knowing to exhaust one's own duty; it is not that one harbors any ulterior hopes. And yet "no blame" and "other good fortune" come about naturally by principle—is this not why the superior man prizes making himself sincere? Even so, how could the meaning of possessing sincerity apply only when engaging in government? Master Qidiao [Qidiao Kai] indeed spoke of it: "In this I am not yet able to have confidence." 聖人之繫辭，因卦之情而已。夫卦之情各有所向，則繫辭者特因而指之爾。此《大傳》釋《易》卦爻辭之通例也。且《易》之爲書，以卦則有小大矣，以辭則有險易矣。然是辭之險易而盡言以告人者不能皆同，亦由卦之小大而趨向之所之者各自以異。凡辭曰凶、曰咎、曰悔吝者，皆險者也，
translation_en:
… presented themselves in advance so as to establish their trustworthiness. Why is this? Only when there is trustworthiness can there be close union, and thus in uniting there is nothing that is not auspicious. Scholars of today are not yet able to have confidence in themselves, yet they rashly harbor an eagerness for rapid advancement; if they wish to escape blame, how could they possibly do so? By this we know that what the Sage calls "sincerity" is spoken of prior to entering into union, and is not something that comes into being only after uniting.

"The appended judgments each point to where one is going."

Yu Maozhong 余懋中

Associate Examiner, Instructor Jiang 蔣, comments: Within its balanced regularity there is an ancient elegance, far surpassing the ordinary tune.
Associate Examiner, Instructor Li 李, comments: The literary meaning is clean and pure—one who is profound in the Book of Changes (Yi 易).
Examiner, Right Admonisher Xu 許, comments: The diction and spirit have a苍然 (venerable and vigorous) quality.
Examiner, Right Companion He 何, comments: Archaic and vigorous.

When the Sages appended the judgments, they simply followed the nature of the hexagrams. Now, since the nature of each hexagram has its own direction toward which it tends, those who appended the judgments merely followed and pointed to it. This is the general principle by which the Great Commentary (Dazhuan 大傳) explains the hexagram and line statements of the Book of Changes. Moreover, as a book, the Changes has hexagrams that are small or great, and judgments that are perilous or easy. Yet the reason these perilous or easy judgments cannot all be identical when exhaustively stated to instruct people is likewise because, depending on whether a hexagram is small or great, the directions toward which they tend each differ from one another. Whenever the judgments say "inauspicious," "blame," "remorse," or "humiliation," they are all perilous; …

title: 萬曆四年順天府鄉試錄
text:
非聖人故危之也卦主於陰其道私而小其所
之也自險故辭亦因而指之惕然示人知懼焉
凡辭曰吉曰亨曰無咎者皆易者也非聖人故
逸之也卦主于陽其道公而大其所之也自易
故辭亦因而指之坦然示人知趨焉雖卦之小
者辭亦有時易矣是蓋天下固有小人而善變
者不得不言易以與其進耳要之小而險者其
常也雖卦之大者辭亦有時險矣是蓋天下固
有君子而用壯者不得不言難以警其後耳要
===
之大而易者其常也危平易傾聖人固以示其
憂世之情然不能外乎卦而創爲之說著于辭
者顯于象矣扶陽抑陰聖人亦未始無衛道之
意然不過因乎卦而預爲之防以言告者以情
遷矣是則分言之則卦與辭殊合觀之則辭因
卦繫知此則卦爻辭之通例可識矣抑聖人之
作易以辭也其得已乎先天立象而意已盡後
乃益之以辭故曰易興于中古作于憂患曰聖
人之情見乎辭吁不得已以辭教天下聖人之

punctuated: 非聖人故危之也。卦主於陰，其道私而小，其所之也自險，故辭亦因而指之，惕然示人知懼焉。凡辭曰「吉」、曰「亨」、曰「無咎」者，皆易者也，非聖人故逸之也。卦主于陽，其道公而大，其所之也自易，故辭亦因而指之，坦然示人知趨焉。雖卦之小者，辭亦有時易矣，是蓋天下固有小人而善變者，不得不言易以與其進耳，要之小而險者其常也。雖卦之大者，辭亦有時險矣，是蓋天下固有君子而用壯者，不得不言難以警其後耳，要之大而易者其常也。危平易傾，聖人固以示其憂世之情，然不能外乎卦而創爲之說，著于辭者顯于象矣。扶陽抑陰，聖人亦未始無衛道之意，然不過因乎卦而預爲之防，以言告者以情遷矣。是則分言之，則卦與辭殊；合觀之，則辭因卦繫。知此則卦爻辭之通例可識矣。抑聖人之作《易》以辭也，其得已乎？先天立象而意已盡，後乃益之以辭。故曰：「《易》興于中古，作于憂患。」曰：「聖人之情見乎辭。」吁！不得已以辭教天下，聖人之
translation_en: … It is not that the sages deliberately made them perilous. When a hexagram is dominated by yin, its way is selfish and petty, and where it goes is naturally treacherous; therefore the appended statements follow this and point it out, vigilantly showing people how to know fear. All statements that speak of "good fortune," "success," or "no blame" are easy ones. It is not that the sages deliberately made them comforting. When a hexagram is dominated by yang, its way is public-spirited and great, and where it goes is naturally smooth; therefore the appended statements follow this and point it out, plainly showing people what course to pursue. Although in petty hexagrams the statements are sometimes easy, this is because in the world there are indeed petty men who are capable of changing for the better, so one cannot but speak of ease in order to encourage their advance; in sum, however, being petty and perilous is their norm. Although in great hexagrams the statements are sometimes perilous, this is because in the world there are indeed superior men who rely on reckless strength, so one cannot but speak of difficulty in order to warn them of what comes after; in sum, however, being great and easy is their norm. Treating the level as perilous and the easy as prone to overturn, the sages certainly used this to display their concern for the world, yet they could not fabricate explanations outside of the hexagrams; what is made manifest in the statements is already revealed in the images. In supporting yang and suppressing yin, the sages were never without the intention of defending the Way, yet they merely followed the hexagrams to establish precautions in advance; what is announced in words shifts according to the inherent tendencies of the hexagrams. Thus, if we speak of them separately, the hexagrams and the statements are distinct; if we view them together, the statements are appended in accordance with the hexagrams. Once one understands this, the general principle of the hexagram and line statements can be recognized. Yet in creating the Changes (Yi) with statements, could the sages have helped doing so? Before Heaven, the images were established and the meaning was already exhausted; only later were statements added to them. Therefore it is said, "The Changes arose in middle antiquity; its authors had anxiety and sorrow," and it is said, "The sentiments of the sages are seen in the statements." Alas! Having no choice but to instruct the world through statements—such was the sages' …

… intent! Why then do those who study the Changes (Yi) fail to savor its words in order to mend their faults, and merely view the Changes as literary expressions? The intent of the sages is thus obscured!

Book of Documents (Shu)

"Gao Yao said: 'Oh! In conduct there are generally nine virtues; and when we say that a man possesses virtue, we mean to say that he initiates such and such deeds.' Yu said: 'What are they?' Gao Yao said: 'Affable yet inspiring awe; mild yet firm; blunt yet respectful; apt for governance yet reverent; docile yet bold; straightforward yet gentle; easy-going yet discerning;刚 [unyielding] yet sincere; strong yet righteous. When these are manifested and maintained with constancy, how auspicious!'"

Wei Yunzhong 魏允中

Moreover, it is rigorous, refined, and pure, with every single word coherently connected—a superb exposition of the Classics.

The great minister broadly outlines the essentials of observing virtue, and thereupon details the substance of perfected virtue. Now, what is prized in virtue is truly possessing it within oneself; when the nine virtues are manifested with constancy, it is certainly perfected virtue. In observing men, what could be more essential than this? In presenting his counsel on knowing men, Gao Yao first exclaims in praise, [saying]…

translation_en:
… taking the knowledge of men as the foremost duty of a ruler, he surely seeks genuine virtue in order to serve practical uses. Yet by what way is this achieved? Although virtue in its all-encompassing profundity issues from a single source, in its visible conduct it generally manifests in nine forms. Still, while possessing virtue is certainly praiseworthy, without verification how can it be trusted? Therefore, merely following reputation will not do; one must thoroughly examine the reality of a person's habitual conduct before our own discernment leaves nothing overlooked. Judging by appearances will not do; one must fully demand that reputation and reality correspond before others can conceal nothing of their true character. This is the essential principle of observing virtue.

When Yu inquired about the specific items, he [Gao Yao] enumerated them all, saying: As for the so-called Nine Virtues, is their value merely in a chance match of talent and nature? Rather, the difficulty lies in their balanced harmony without one-sidedness. Thus, there is breadth and magnanimity combined with reverent dignity, and gentle compliance combined with firm independence; as for cautious sincerity together with administrative talent, they are further combined with respectful diligence and reverent awe. There is docile tractability combined with resolute boldness, straightforwardness combined with mild geniality, and easy simplicity combined with scrupulous integrity; as for unyielding strength [and?] vigorous courage, they are further combined with steadfastness and a love of righteousness. Those who are deep and reserved are never without firm mastery, [and] those who are lofty and brilliant are never without gentle mastery—this is what constitutes the Nine Virtues.

Truly, if those who possess these virtues both manifest them fully in their practical conduct according to the measure they hold, and maintain them consistently from beginning to end without altering their permanently upright resolve, then their cultivation follows the proper Way, and they stand out as renowned heroes of the age; their perfected virtue becomes their conduct, and they are truly accomplished men of pure cultivation. What else could they be called if not "auspicious gentlemen" (jishi)? Ah! This is what is meant by "performing deeds upon deeds," and thus calling them men of virtue is no empty claim. If a ruler selects men by this standard, what difficulty would there be in knowing them, and in appointing them to office what…

「五、皇極。皇建其有極，斂時五福，用敷錫厥庶民。惟時厥庶民于汝極，錫汝保極。凡厥庶民，無有淫朋，人無有比德，惟皇作極。」

translation_en:
… fail to be fittingly placed? Examining the era of Yu (Shun), below there arose a custom of esteeming conduct, while above they emphasized a governance of gathering substantive deeds; thus there was good reason that worthy talents flourished and transformative rule prospered. In later ages, scholarship and human talent were already not equal to antiquity, and the methods of selection and evaluation moreover did not focus exclusively on moral virtue, instead selecting for talent and artistic skill—how then could the Sovereign Way be upheld? What should those who desire good governance do? It can only be said: follow the teaching of the "three things" (sanwu) of the Accomplished Zhou in order to restore the selection by the "nine virtues" (jiude) of the court of Yu, and only then will it be possible.

"Fifth, the August Ultimate. The Sovereign establishes his supreme standard; he gathers together these Five Blessings, and thereby diffuses and bestows them upon his common people. Then the common people, resting in your supreme standard, will bestow upon you the preservation of this standard. Among all the common people, there shall be no licentious factions, and among men in office there shall be no collusive practices; only let the Sovereign establish the supreme standard."

Associate Examiner Instructor Luo comments: It brings out the principle of ruler and people forming a single body; intimate and praiseworthy.
Associate Examiner Metropolitan Graduate Ji comments: It skillfully grasps the meaning of establishing the supreme standard, and expresses it in ancient, elegant, and vigorous language; none without both learning and insight could achieve this.
Examiner Right Admonisher Xu comments: Harmonious, integrated, poised, and refined.
Examiner Right Companion He comments: It grasps the essential purport.

When the noble man (Jizi) expounded the category of the August Ultimate, there was the transformative influence by which the supreme standard is established, and there was the foundation by which that transformation is brought to completion. For the ruler is the standard for subjects and people. Proceeding from the transformation of their mutual responsiveness to trace back…

title: 萬曆四年順天府鄉試錄
text:
化成之本觀之而極豈可以不建哉箕子告武
王意謂禹於疇之中數而第之以皇極是極之
所係大矣而建用之義何居彼皇履天下之上
本斯世所取衷也必位在德元中天地而爲綱
常之主議道自己統民物以立紀法之宗則善
氣迎而天休滋至太和召而百順駢臻福其有
不隨者乎然君之歛福非獨厚其身也即是極
以敷錫焉而君盖有以與乎民矣民之被福非
無與於君也即是極以錫保焉而民遂有以與
===
乎君矣君民相與而實相因如此化成之本豈
在外哉吾知觀俗於野而無淫朋是民保君之
極也而非民自能也惟皇昭大中以樹之軌故
民自從乂焉耳否則安能靡然向風若是耶觀
政於朝而無比德是臣保君之極也而非臣自
能也惟皇守至正以示之趨故臣自欽若焉耳
否則安能翕然不變若是耶吁皇極之理通於
下而歸極之機係於上信乎建用之不容已也
極建而彝倫有不敘者哉大抵治天下之道九

translation_en: … the basis by which transformation is accomplished, how could the ultimate standard not be established? What Jizi meant in instructing King Wu was this: At the central number of the categories, Yu ranked the Royal Perfection; thus what depends upon this ultimate standard is great indeed—yet wherein lies the meaning of establishing and employing it? The sovereign occupies the supreme position over the world and is fundamentally the one from whom this age takes its standard of judgment. He must occupy the首位 of primal virtue, standing at the center of Heaven and Earth as the master of the cardinal guides and constant virtues; he must deliberate on the Way from within himself, governing the people and all things so as to set up the foundation of laws and regulations. Then auspicious influences will be welcomed and heavenly blessings will arrive in abundance; supreme harmony will be summoned and a hundred felicities will gather together—how could good fortune fail to follow? Yet when the ruler concentrates these五福 blessings, it is not merely to enrich his own person; by means of this very standard he spreads and bestows them, and thus the ruler truly shares them with the people. And when the people receive blessings, it is not without connection to the ruler; by means of this very standard they preserve what is bestowed upon them, and thus the people in turn respond to the ruler. Since ruler and people interact and in fact mutually depend on one another in this way, how could the basis of accomplishing transformation lie outside? I know that when one observes customs in the countryside and sees no licentious factions, this is the people preserving the ruler's ultimate standard—yet it is not something the people are capable of by themselves. Only because the sovereign manifests the Great Mean to set up a model for them do the people naturally follow and become well-governed; otherwise, how could they incline toward his moral influence so uniformly as this? When one observes governance at court and sees no partisan cabals, this is the ministers preserving the ruler's ultimate standard—yet it is not something the ministers are capable of by themselves. Only because the sovereign upholds the Utmost Correctness to show them the direction do the ministers naturally revere and accord with it; otherwise, how could they remain so harmoniously unchanged as this? Ah! The principle of Royal Perfection extends throughout those below, while the pivot of returning to the standard rests with the one above; truly, the establishing and employing of it cannot be neglected! Once the standard is established, how could the invariant human relationships fail to be set in order? Broadly speaking, the Way of governing the world is exhausted by the Nine …

translation_en:
… Nine Categories exhaust it; and as for the profound meaning of the Nine Categories, the Royal Perfection serves as its guiding cord. This is why establishing the standard of perfection is essential. Yet an emperor or king has a standard of perfection in his person, and a standard of perfection in his mind. If the mind is not pure, how can that perfection be established? Therefore it is said: "The sage settles it with centrality, correctness, humaneness, and righteousness, and regards tranquility as fundamental, thus establishing the ultimate standard of humanity." Now, the standard of regarding tranquility as fundamental is the standard of perfection of the mind, from which all transformations issue forth. May he who rules the world seek the beginning here!

title: 萬曆四年順天府鄉試錄
text:
詩人美周士之生爲王國之本夫國之所恃以
立者人也多士生王國而其本固矣聖世得人
之盛如此周公陳祖德于王而以命周之福言
之意謂周士翼猶以顯世豈偶然哉蓋天實啓
之爲我周計耳美哉多士天地清淑之氣其鍾
也不數明良交際之期其遘也甚難本所自生
帝命之維新乃賚而弼焉於此王國文德之丕
顯如待而興焉若是者在異代尚亦有賴况其
時乎得一人已足爲重况其多乎今王國而能
===
生之也將見疏附在是先後在是岐之山若增
而高奔奏在是禦侮在是渭之水若增而深昭
事上帝承天休者素矣雖天之難諶而國有人
焉足以培昌祚於不拔猶垣之有榦而植以爲
基也怙冒西土結民心者厚矣雖民之易渙而
國有人焉足以保洪業於無疆猶築之有基而
附以爲固也噫周士之爲楨於國如此其傳世
之顯固宜雖然士之爲國楨也非獨自樹蓋本
人君造就之力焉夫天之生才何代無之彼周

punctuated: 詩人美周士之生，爲王國之本。夫國之所恃以立者，人也。多士生王國，而其本固矣。聖世得人之盛如此。周公陳祖德于王，而以命周之福言之，意謂周士翼猶以顯世，豈偶然哉？蓋天實啓之，爲我周計耳。美哉多士！天地清淑之氣，其鍾也不數；明良交際之期，其遘也甚難。本所自生，帝命之維新，乃賚而弼焉；於此王國，文德之丕顯，如待而興焉。若是者，在異代尚亦有賴，况其時乎？得一人已足爲重，况其多乎？今王國而能生之也，將見疏附在是，先後在是，岐之山若增而高；奔奏在是，禦侮在是，渭之水若增而深。昭事上帝，承天休者素矣，雖天之難諶，而國有人焉，足以培昌祚於不拔，猶垣之有榦，而植以爲基也；怙冒西土，結民心者厚矣，雖民之易渙，而國有人焉，足以保洪業於無疆，猶築之有基，而附以爲固也。噫！周士之爲楨於國如此，其傳世之顯固宜。雖然，士之爲國楨也，非獨自樹，蓋本人君造就之力焉。夫天之生才，何代無之？彼周…
translation_en:
The poet praises the birth of the gentlemen of Zhou as the foundation of the royal state. Now, that upon which a state relies to stand is its people. When the many gentlemen are born in the royal state, its foundation is made firm. Such was the flourishing abundance of worthy men obtained in a sacred age.

When the Duke of Zhou set forth the ancestral virtues before the King and spoke of the blessings of the Mandate conferred upon Zhou, his meaning was: how could it be by mere chance that the gentlemen of Zhou assisted in grand counsels and became illustrious for generations? Indeed, Heaven truly opened the way for this, planning on behalf of our Zhou. Admirable indeed are the many gentlemen! The pure and benignvital energy of Heaven and Earth is not often concentrated in one place; the moment of encounter between an enlightened ruler and worthy ministers is exceedingly hard to meet. Originating from where they were born, as the Lord on High’s Mandate was renewed, they were bestowed to give aid; in this royal state, the great splendor of civil virtue arose as if awaiting them. Men such as these would be relied upon even in another dynasty—how much more so in their own time! Obtaining even one such man is enough to bring weight to the state—how much more so when there are many!

Now, since the royal state was able to bring them forth, one would see that those who draw the estranged to attach themselves are here, and those who guide from before and behind are here—Mount Qi seems to gain in height; those who hasten about in service are here, and those who repel insults are here—the Wei River seems to gain in depth. In brightly serving the Lord on High, the state had long received Heaven’s blessings; although Heaven is hard to rely upon with certainty, when the state possesses such men, they suffice to cultivate a prosperous line so that it cannot be uprooted, just as a wall has wooden framing-posts planted to serve as its foundation. In sheltering and overspreading the Western Lands, the state had deeply bound the hearts of the people; although the people are easily scattered, when the state possesses such men, they suffice to preserve the great enterprise without bound, just as rammed earth has a base to which it adheres for solidity.

Ah! Since the gentlemen of Zhou served as framing-posts for the state in this manner, it was certainly fitting that their renown was handed down through the generations. Even so, that gentlemen become framing-posts of the state is not solely through their own self-establishment; it is rooted in the ruler’s power of nurturing and forming them. After all, in what age does Heaven not give birth to talent? Those… [of Zhou]…

之多士，非商之遺黎乎？作以《菁莪》、《棫樸》，寄以《干城》腹心，則文王之所以爲楨者，乃文王自爲之也。故曰：「人主愛惜人才，自爲社稷計。」信夫！

「商邑翼翼，四方之極。」
陸鯉
同考試官教諭姚批：體勢尊大，詞氣嚴整，末歸本聖武，尤見知要。
同考試官教諭王批：以簡古之詞，發平實之理，可式。
同考試官學正郝批：此題作者多分截，殊非語意。是作一氣串下，而詞旨謹嚴，卓有中興氣象。
同考試官學正陳批：雄偉簡嚴，當於古作求之。

觀王畿之勢尊，見中興之道振。夫王畿者，天下之本也。而翼然爲四方極焉，商道其復振乎！此高宗中興之頌也。蓋曰：昔我成湯，奄有四方，爰
translation_en:
… many officers—were they not the surviving populace of Shang? Cultivated in the manner of the odes "Luxuriant Tarragon" (Jing'e) and "Luxuriant Scrub-Oak" (Yupu), and entrusted as "shields and walls, hearts and minds" (gancheng fuxin), those who served as the pillars for King Wen were in fact forged by King Wen himself. Thus it is said: "When a ruler cherishes men of talent, he is planning for the altars of soil and grain on his own behalf." Truly is it so!

"The capital of Shang was in careful order, the standard for the four quarters."
Lu Li 陸鯉
Associate Examiner, Instructor Yao 姚 comments: Its structure and momentum are dignified and grand, and its diction and tone are rigorous and orderly. At the end, it traces the root back to sagely martial prowess, which especially shows a grasp of the essentials.
Associate Examiner, Instructor Wang 王 comments: Using concise and archaic diction to expound plain and solid principles, it can serve as a model.
Associate Examiner, Subprefectural Director of Studies Hao 郝 comments: Writers on this topic mostly divide it into separate segments, which is quite contrary to the meaning of the words. This piece flows continuously in a single breath, while its diction and purport are rigorous and strict, outstandingly possessing the spirit of a dynastic revival.
Associate Examiner, Subprefectural Director of Studies Chen 陳 comments: Majestic, concise, and rigorous; one must seek its like among ancient compositions.
Examiner, Right Admonisher Xu 許 comments: Grave and dignified.
Examiner, Right Companion He 何 comments: Refined and pure.

Observing the dignified position of the royal domain, one sees the revival of the Way of restoration. Now, the royal domain is the foundation of All under Heaven. When it stands in careful order as the standard for the four quarters, is not the Way of Shang revived once more? This is a eulogy on the restoration under Gaozong 高宗. It says in effect: In antiquity, our Tang the Successful 成湯 comprehensively possessed the four quarters, and thereupon…

title: 萬曆四年順天府鄉試錄
text:
蔡侯鄭伯會于鄧〔桓公二年〕楚人伐鄭〔莊〕
〔公元年〕
王士琦
同考試官進士張批嚴整瑩潔發聖人經
世之畧盡矣宜錄以式
考試官右贊善許批事核詞嚴
考試官右中允何批得謹嚴體
春秋志内弱外强之事而經世之慮深焉此見
列國始戒心于楚而楚之馮陵益張經斯世者
===
可弗慮哉蓋聞中國居内象易之陽焉而易于
陽德方隆猶示以莧陸之决則無乃防病夷之
漸乎春秋感夫鄧之會巳曰自新田菑畝之事
遠而華風不競于南醞釀至魯桓之世王靈霸
業兩俱虛而勢彌弱矣三國之近楚也同懼而
會鄧也獨不聞壇好之間有陳玉而悲者乎急
懼人而緩修治吾見其策無良也噫四夷方視
内之强以銷萌也而今則何如哉厥後鄧滅蔡
俘驅懿親而服之役聖人故傷之也始庸知矣

春秋志內弱外強之事而經世之慮深焉此見
===

遠而華風不競于南甌釀至魯桓之世王靈霸

punctuated:
蔡侯、鄭伯會于鄧〔桓公二年〕；楚人伐鄭〔莊公元年〕。
王士琦
同考試官進士張批：嚴整瑩潔，發聖人經世之畧盡矣，宜錄以式。
考試官右贊善許批：事核詞嚴。
考試官右中允何批：得謹嚴體。
《春秋》志内弱外强之事，而經世之慮深焉。此見列國始戒心于楚，而楚之馮陵益張，經斯世者可弗慮哉！蓋聞中國居内，象《易》之陽焉；而《易》于陽德方隆，猶示以莧陸之决，則無乃防病夷之漸乎？《春秋》感夫鄧之會，巳曰：自新田菑畝之事遠，而華風不競于南，醞釀至魯桓之世，王靈霸業兩俱虛，而勢彌弱矣。三國之近楚也，同懼而會鄧也，獨不聞壇好之間，有陳玉而悲者乎？急懼人而緩修治，吾見其策無良也。噫！四夷方視内之强以銷萌也，而今則何如哉？厥後鄧滅蔡俘，驅懿親而服之役，聖人故傷之也。始庸知矣……
translation_en:
"The Marquis of Cai and the Earl of Zheng met at Deng" [Second year of Duke Huan]; "The people of Chu invaded Zheng" [First year of Duke Zhuang].

Wang Shiqi 王士琦

Associate Examiner, the metropolitan graduate (jinshi) Zhang, comments: Rigorous, well-ordered, and limpid; it has fully brought out the Sage's strategy for ordering the world, and ought to be recorded as a model.
Examiner, Left or Right Admonisher (You Zanshan) Xu, comments: Factually precise and severe in diction.
Examiner, Right Companion (You Zhongyun) He, comments: Captures the style of strictness and rigor.

The Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu) records the affairs of internal weakness and external strength, and in doing so its concern for ordering the world is profound. Here we see the various states beginning to take alarm at Chu, while Chu's encroachments and arrogance grew ever more rampant—how could one who orders this world not be concerned! For I have heard that the Central States occupy the interior, symbolizing the yang of the Book of Changes (Yi); yet even when the virtue of yang is at its height, the Changes still gives the admonition of cutting off the pokeweed (xianlu), is this not to guard against the gradual onset of harm from the barbarians? Being moved by the meeting at Deng, the Spring and Autumn Annals says in effect: Ever since the campaigns of newly cleared fields and first-year acreage grew distant in the past, the prestige of Hua (China) has failed to prevail in the south; brewing down to the age of Duke Huan of Lu, royal authority and hegemonic enterprise were both alike empty, and their position grew ever weaker. The three states, being close to Chu, shared a common fear and met at Deng—yet had they alone not heard that amidst the friendly meeting at the altar there was one who laid out jade and wept? Urgent in fearing others while slow to cultivate their own governance—I see that they had no sound plan. Alas! The four barbarian tribes look precisely to the strength of the interior to quell their nascent ambitions, yet how did things stand now? Thereafter Deng was extinguished and Cai taken captive, driving close royal kin into servitude—therefore the Sage grieved over it. How could one have known from the beginning [reading 矣 as 天: that Heaven (?) would not inspire us to punish the jackals and wolves]…

title: 萬曆四年順天府鄉試錄
text:
之不啓我以罰豺狼而奈之何其偷也又聞夷
狄居外象易之陰焉而易于陰孽初形輒示以
金柅之繫則無乃杜猾夏之階乎春秋感夫鄭
之伐巳曰自方城漢水之疆分而荆氣洊雄于
北浸淫至魯僖之世長主賢臣兩相得而勢彌
强矣鄭方即于夏也楚遂討其違也獨不聞軍
興之際有投袂而忿者乎名虐鄭而實撓霸吾
見其心無巳也噫諸夏方視外之弱以持安也
而今則何如哉厥後主會受朝脅宗盟而奪之
===
長聖人故謹之也始庸知天之不授彼以勸親
暱而奈之何其忽也噫春秋經世之慮何深哉
大抵天下無常强無常弱御得其道則强在内
御失其道則强在外御之不可不慎也當是時
周政失而楚之竊發所繇來乆列國奚責乎後
世儒者論御夷之道曰其備不在邊境而在朝
廷誠善發春秋之旨
楚公子嬰齊帥師伐莒庚申莒潰楚遂入
鄆〔成公九年〕

punctuated:
之不啓我以罰豺狼，而奈之何其偷也？又聞夷狄居外，象《易》之陰焉；而《易》于陰孽初形，輒示以「金柅之繫」，則無乃杜猾夏之階乎？《春秋》感夫鄭之伐巳，曰：自方城、漢水之疆分，而荆氣洊雄于北，浸淫至魯僖之世，長主賢臣兩相得，而勢彌强矣。鄭方即于夏也，楚遂討其違也。獨不聞軍興之際，有投袂而忿者乎？名虐鄭而實撓霸，吾見其心無巳也。噫！諸夏方視外之弱以持安也，而今則何如哉？厥後主會受朝，脅宗盟而奪之長，聖人故謹之也。始庸知天之不授彼以勸親暱，而奈之何其忽也？噫！《春秋》經世之慮，何深哉！大抵天下無常强、無常弱：御得其道，則强在内；御失其道，則强在外。御之不可不慎也。當是時，周政失，而楚之竊發所繇來乆，列國奚責乎？後世儒者論御夷之道，曰：「其備不在邊境，而在朝廷。」誠善發《春秋》之旨。
楚公子嬰齊帥師伐莒。庚申，莒潰。楚遂入鄆。〔成公九年〕
translation_en:
… did not inspire us to punish the wolves and jackals, so how could they be so lax? I have also heard that the barbarians dwelling on the outside correspond to the yin principle in the Book of Changes (Yi 易); and when the sprout of yin first takes form, the Book of Changes immediately warns of "tying it to a metal brake." Is this not to block the steps by which they might throw the central states (Xia 夏) into disorder? The Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu 春秋), moved by the campaign against Zheng, says in effect: Ever since the borders of Fangcheng and the Han River were demarcated, the spirit of Jing [Chu] repeatedly grew mighty toward the north; spreading gradually down to the reign of Duke Xi of Lu, an elder ruler and worthy ministers found mutual accord, and their power became stronger still. Just as Zheng was aligning itself with the central states, Chu thereupon punished its defection. Had they alone not heard that, when the armies were raised, there was one who flung his sleeve in indignation? Nominally it was toharry Zheng, but in reality it was to thwart the霸 (hegemon); I see that their ambition knew no end. Alas! The central states were just then looking to the weakness of the outside to maintain their own security—yet how do things stand now? Thereafter, Chu presided over covenants and received court visits, coercing the kinsmen of the royal house in alliance and seizing the leadership from them; the Sage therefore recorded this with caution. In the beginning, how could one know that Heaven was not empowering them in order to admonish the royal kinsmen to draw close to one another—so how could they be so negligent? Alas, how profound are the Spring and Autumn Annals' considerations for ordering the world! On the whole, in the world there is no permanent strength and no permanent weakness: when governed according to the proper Way, strength lies within; when governed without the proper Way, strength lies without. In governing them, one cannot but be cautious. At that time, the governance of Zhou had failed, and the covert rise of Chu had been coming about for a long time; how could the various feudal states alone be blamed? When Confucian scholars of later ages discussed the Way of governing barbarians, they said: "Defense against them lies not at the frontier, but in the court." Truly, this well brings out the purport of the Spring and Autumn Annals.

Prince Yingqi of Chu led a force to attack Ju. On the gengshen day, Ju collapsed. Chu thereupon entered Yun. [Ninth year of Duke Cheng]

有死忠之分耳嗟乎地利不如人和蓋自古記
