《禮記》

天子乃以元日祈穀于上帝。乃擇元辰，天子親載耒耜，措之于參保介之御間，帥三公、九卿、諸侯、大夫，躬耕帝籍。
translation_en:
… if the city walls cannot repel the enemy, how can we repel the enemy?" Thus they abandon them without looking back, never even knowing that they have a duty to die in loyalty. Alas! That geographical advantage is not as good as human harmony has indeed been recorded since antiquity. When the people are not harmonious and yet one repairs the city walls, the people will not bear the toil. If they toil and resent it, this breeds disloyalty. If the city walls are merely intact while the people are exhausted, the people will not devote themselves to their defense. When they abandon them and flee, one has merely erected empty battlements. Even if Ju had been able to fortify its three cities, how could it have escaped a total rout?

At the rout of Ju, the Classic records the day as a warning, wishing that those who possess states would not rely on terrain, but rather value Heaven's principle—dwelling in the exalted position while preserving the dread of "upon whom can I rely?", and overseeing those below while illuminating the hardship of having "none to whom to appeal." Thereby an unseen bulwark is made firm, and the state enjoys lasting order. When this meaning was obscured, those in the world who worried about external aggression often drained the fat and blood of the people for the work of building walls and moats, not knowing that when the work of building walls and moats becomes burdensome, it only deepens the worries of the state. Take those who walled Ying, yet Wu ultimately entered; or those who dug a moat around the palace, yet Liang finally perished—were they not well-prepared? Well spoken were the words of the Han minister: "A worthy ruler alone observes the source of the myriad transformations, cultivates it in the ancestral temple and court, and dissolves disasters before they take form; the essential point is simply to ensure that the realm has no tendency toward crumbling like earth."

Record of Rites (Liji)

"The Son of Heaven on the first Hsin day prays for grain to the Supreme Ruler. Then, choosing an auspicious Ch'en day, the Son of Heaven personally carries the plowshare and handle, placing them between the third rider—the Assistant Protector—and the charioteer, and leads the Three Dukes, the Nine Ministers, the feudal lords, and the Great Officers to personally plow the Imperial Field."

沈季文
同考試官進士方批題㫖融洽文氣渾成
非邃于禮學者不到此
考試官右賛善許批敬天勤民原非二事此作
得之
考試官右中允何批發揮明透
王者舉祈年之典而因有事於耕籍焉夫祈年
以仁民也耕籍以敬神也王者日而行之其知
急先務者乎且人君協上下以承休敬天勤民
===
之責胥萃焉者也時維孟春帝出乎震而東作
之期肇矣天子將何為哉有見於民以食為天
而五穀之生則自上帝以宰其化也乃因元日
之臨而肆舉夫燔柴之節行祈穀之禮而仰兾
夫默相之功兆於南郊祝西成也通之以明信
而降康者可卜矣從以后稷望有秋也孚之以
精禋而粒食者攸賴矣斯固天子之靈承於上
帝而造福於生民者也然是穀也耕者之所獲
也亦祭之所以供粢盛也是耕也小人之所依

王者舉祈年之典而因有事於耕籍焉夫祈年
以仁民也耕籍以敬神也王者日而行之其知
急先務者乎且人君協上下以承休敬天勤民
===
之責胥萃焉者也時維孟春帝出乎震而東作
之期肇矣天子將何爲哉有見於民以食爲天
而五穀之生則自上帝以宰其化也乃因元日
之臨而肆舉夫燔柴之儀行祈穀之禮而仰冀
夫默相之功兆於南郊祝西成也通之以明信
而降康者可卜矣從以后稷望有秋也孚之以
精禋而粒食者攸賴矣斯固天子之靈承於上
帝而造福於生民者也然是穀也耕者之所獲
也亦祭之所以供粢盛也是耕也小人之所依
punctuated:
沈季文

考試官右中允何批：發揮明透。

王者舉祈年之典，而因有事於耕籍焉。夫祈年，以仁民也；耕籍，以敬神也。王者日而行之，其知急先務者乎！且人君協上下以承休，敬天勤民之責胥萃焉者也。時維孟春，帝出乎震，而東作之期肇矣，天子將何為哉？有見於民以食為天，而五穀之生，則自上帝以宰其化也。乃因元日之臨，而肆舉夫燔柴之節，行祈穀之禮，而仰兾夫默相之功。兆於南郊，祝西成也，通之以明信，而降康者可卜矣；從以后稷，望有秋也，孚之以精禋，而粒食者攸賴矣。斯固天子之靈承於上帝，而造福於生民者也。然是穀也，耕者之所獲也，亦祭之所以供粢盛也；是耕也，小人之所依…
translation_en:
Shen Jiwen 沈季文
Associate Examiner, Metropolitan Graduate (jinshi) Fang 方 comments: The purport of the theme is harmoniously integrated and the literary vigor is seamlessly formed; no one who is not profound in the study of ritual could attain this.
Examiner, Right Admonisher Xu 許 comments: Revering Heaven and being diligent toward the people are originally not two separate matters; this composition grasps it.
Examiner, Right Companion He 何 comments: The elaboration is clear and penetrating.

The true king performs the ceremony of praying for a good year, and consequently engages in the ritual of plowing the sacred field. Now, praying for a good year is out of benevolence toward the people; plowing the sacred field is out of reverence for the spirits. When the true king carries these out by selecting the proper days, does he not know how to attend urgently to the foremost duties? Moreover, the ruler of men harmonizes those above and below in order to receive blessings; the responsibilities of revering Heaven and being diligent toward the people both converge in him. When the season is the first month of spring, the Lord emerges in the east [Zhen], and the period of spring farming begins—what then shall the Son of Heaven do? He observes that the people regard food as their heaven, and that the growth of the five grains stems from the Lord on High, who governs their transformation. Therefore, upon the arrival of the auspicious first day [shangxin], he grandly performs the rite of burning firewood on the altar, conducting the ceremony of praying for grain and looking up in hope of the merit of silent aid. Performing the sacrifice at the altar in the southern suburbs is to pray for the autumn harvest; communicating with bright sincerity, the sending down of prosperity can be divined. Associating Hou Ji in the sacrifice is to hope for an abundant autumn; inspiring trust through pure burnt offerings, those who subsist on grain have that upon which they rely. This is indeed how the Son of Heaven reverently responds to the Lord on High and creates blessings for the living people. Yet this grain is what the plowman reaps, and also that by which the sacrificial vessels are supplied with millet for offerings; this plowing is what the common people depend upon…

title: 萬曆四年順天府鄉試錄
text:
也亦天子之所以事上帝也乃擇元辰而天時
協矣親載耒耜以措於參保介御之間而物曲
備矣於是帥彼三公九卿焉從廟堂以親畎畝
之事而小大莫處凡以服其勤也帥彼諸侯大
夫焉奉萬乘以即千畝之勞而貴賤皆御無敢
愛其力也載之既祈而此則開稼穡之始帝之
既享而此則昭黍稷之馨豈曰莫爲之耕哉是
其始也以農之故而祈乎神其既也以神之故
而親乎農王政之急先務如此固宜民懷其仁
===
神歆其德歟大抵月令所紀皆周家之制吾觀
載芟之篇言成王周公耕籍以勸農祈社以求
穀故其民樂田畝而屢豐年王業之興信不偶
也噫此既耕小郊獻子非之而不籍千畝文公
以爲諫歟有天下者可以省矣
故男子生桑弧蓬矢六以射天地四方天
地四方者男子之所有事也故必先有
志於其所有事然後敢用穀也飯食之
謂也

punctuated:
也，亦天子之所以事上帝也。乃擇元辰而天時協矣，親載耒耜，以措於參保介御之間，而物曲備矣。於是帥彼三公、九卿焉，從廟堂以親畎畝之事，而小大莫處，凡以服其勤也；帥彼諸侯、大夫焉，奉萬乘以即千畝之勞，而貴賤皆御，無敢愛其力也。載之既祈，而此則開稼穡之始；帝之既享，而此則昭黍稷之馨，豈曰莫爲之耕哉！是其始也，以農之故而祈乎神；其既也，以神之故而親乎農。王政之急先務如此，固宜民懷其仁、神歆其德歟！大抵《月令》所紀，皆周家之制。吾觀《載芟》之篇，言成王、周公耕籍以勸農，祈社以求穀，故其民樂田畝而屢豐年，王業之興，信不偶也。噫！此既耕小郊，獻子非之；而不籍千畝，文公以爲諫歟！有天下者可以省矣。

「故男子生，桑弧蓬矢六，以射天地四方。天地四方者，男子之所有事也。故必先有志於其所有事，然後敢用穀也，飯食之謂也。」
translation_en:
… and is also the means by which the Son of Heaven serves the Lord on High. Thereupon he selects an auspicious morning, and the season of Heaven is in harmony; he personally carries the plowshare and handle, placing them between the third rider—his armed attendant—and the charioteer, and the requisite implements are thoroughly prepared. Thereupon he leads those Three Dukes and Nine Ministers, going from the ancestral temple and court to personally attend to the work of the furrowed fields, so that neither great nor small remain idle at home, all in order to devote themselves to its toil; he leads those feudal lords and grand masters, attending the sovereign of ten thousand chariots to take up the labor of the thousand-mou ritual field, so that noble and base alike are in attendance, none daring to spare his strength. Having already offered prayers at the outset of spring, by this act he initiates the beginning of sowing and reaping; the Lord on High having already accepted the sacrifice, by this act he manifests the fragrant offering of millet—how could it be said that no one plows for it! Thus, at first, for the sake of agriculture he prays to the spirits; thereafter, for the sake of the spirits he personally engages in agriculture. When kingly governance treats its foremost duties with such urgency, is it not fitting indeed that the people cherish his benevolence and the spirits delight in his virtue?

On the whole, what is recorded in the "Monthly Ordinances" (Yueling) are all institutions of the house of Zhou. When I examine the ode "Clearing the Grass" (Zai shan), it speaks of King Cheng and the Duke of Zhou plowing the imperial ritual field to encourage agriculture and praying to the altars of soil and grain to ask for a good harvest; therefore their people delighted in the fields and repeatedly enjoyedyears of abundance—the flourishing of kingly enterprise was truly no accident. Alas! Is this not why, when the suburban sacrifice was divined [?] after the plowing had already taken place, Meng Xianzi孟獻子 criticized it; and when the king failed to plow the thousand-mou ritual field, Duke Wen of Guo 虢文公 remonstrated against it? Those who possess the Empire may well reflect on this!

"Therefore, when a boy is born, a bow of mulberry wood and six arrows of fleabane are used to shoot toward heaven, earth, and the four quarters. Heaven, earth, and the four quarters are the sphere of a man's endeavors. Thus he must first set his ambition upon that to which he will devote his endeavors, and only then dare to partake of grain—which refers to being fed."

text:
韓子祁
同考試官進士方批聯絡有情發揮透徹
是當不愧于始射之義者
考試官右賛善許批是可以觀志

始射之有所期觀諸臣道而自見矣夫人臣以
先事後祿為忠也始生之用射不有見於此哉
且天下之事慎其初君子之志務其大夫人未
有期之不豫而能有所副者也吾觀始射之義
矣是故男子之生也以父母愛之之心莫有先
於食之者而今以桑弧一焉蓬矢六焉而為天
地四方之射何哉蓋以天地之大四方之廣必
得人以任其責而彌綸天地之道綱紀四方之
治微男子無以效其能雖一人之身而宇宙萃
焉不可以他辭也雖六合之事而職分關焉不
可以自諉也始射之義如此而所以期之者不
小矣是以男子之出而為臣正將以行吾天地
四方之志而非以適己之私也故必先盡忠□

同考試官、進士方，批：「聯絡有情，發揮透徹，是當不愧于始射之義者。」
考試官、右賛善許，批：「是可以觀志。」

始射之有所期，觀諸臣道而自見矣。夫人臣以先事後祿為忠也，始生之用射，不有見於此哉？且天下之事慎其初，君子之志務其大，夫人未有期之不豫而能有所副者也，吾觀始射之義矣。是故男子之生也，以父母愛之之心，莫有先於食之者；而今以桑弧一焉、蓬矢六焉，而為天地四方之射，何哉？蓋以天地之大、四方之廣，必得人以任其責；而彌綸天地之道、綱紀四方之治，微男子無以效其能。雖一人之身，而宇宙萃焉，不可以他辭也；雖六合之事，而職分關焉，不可以自諉也。始射之義如此，而所以期之者不小矣。是以男子之出而為臣，正將以行吾天地四方之志，而非以適己之私也。故必先盡忠□
translation_en:
Han Ziqi 韓子祁
Associate Examiner, metropolitan graduate (jinshi) Fang 方, comments: "Well-connected with genuine feeling, and thoroughly developed in its exposition; this truly does justice to the meaning of the inaugural archery rite."
Examiner, Right Admonisher Xu 許, comments: "From this one may observe his aspiration."
Examiner, Right Companion He 何, comments: "Fluent and expressive."

That there is an expectation in the inaugural archery rite becomes self-evident when viewed in light of the Way of the minister. Now, a minister regards putting service first and emolument second as loyalty; does not the use of archery at birth reflect an insight into this? Moreover, in the affairs of the world one must be careful at their beginning, and the aspirations of a gentleman must be directed toward what is great. Never has anyone failed to set expectations beforehand and yet been able to fulfill them; I see this in the meaning of the inaugural archery rite.

Therefore, when a boy is born, given his parents' love for him, nothing should take precedence over feeding him. Yet now they take a single bow of mulberry wood and six arrows of fleabane to shoot toward Heaven, Earth, and the four directions—why is this? It is because given the vastness of Heaven and Earth and the breadth of the four directions, there must be men found to shoulder the responsibility for them; and as for encompassing the Way of Heaven and Earth and ordering the governance of the four directions, without men there is no means to bring such abilities into effect. Though he is but a single person, the universe converges in him, and he cannot decline it by shifting it to others; though these are the affairs of the six directions of the cosmos, his own duty is bound up with them, and he cannot shirk them himself. Such is the meaning of the inaugural archery rite, and what is expected of him through it is no small thing. Therefore, when a man goes forth to become a minister, it is precisely in order to carry out his aspirations toward Heaven, Earth, and the four directions, and not to gratify his own private interests. Thus he must first exhaust his loyalty [?] …

title: 萬曆四年順天府鄉試錄
text:
裁成左右之功而後敢食君之祿也使職之曠
而惟素餐則以爲懼矣或效未集而先受賜亦
以爲耻矣若此者豈自今日得之哉正始生飯
食之謂耳其先射而後食者期所副也慈父以
保其子而豫養乎大人之具是臣鵠之立也其
先事而後穀者副所期也忠臣以事其君而不
失乎赤子之心是男敎之體也吾觀始生之射
而知所以作忠矣射之時義大矣哉自正誼明
道之學不講而功利之感人深也由志之不定
===

其所謂思兼思匹夫匹婦不獲思天下之飢溺
其志曷甞不在天地四方夫是以胼胝不辭而
憂勤罔恤也利祿云乎哉故曰射者繹已之志
也此又定志之說也

punctuated:
裁成左右之功，而後敢食君之祿也。使職之曠而惟素餐，則以爲懼矣；或效未集而先受賜，亦以爲耻矣。若此者，豈自今日得之哉？正始生飯食之謂耳。其先射而後食者，期所副也，慈父以保其子，而豫養乎大人之具，是臣鵠之立也；其先事而後穀者，副所期也，忠臣以事其君，而不失乎赤子之心，是男敎之體也。吾觀始生之射，而知所以作忠矣。射之時義大矣哉！自正誼明道之學不講，而功利之感人深也，由志之不定耳。禹、稷、伊、周，以聖輔聖，勳業章章著矣。然夷考其所謂思兼、思匹夫匹婦不獲、思天下之飢溺，其志曷甞不在天地四方？夫是以胼胝不辭，而憂勤罔恤也，利祿云乎哉！故曰：「射者，繹已之志也。」此又定志之說也。

第貳塲
論
《天人相與之際》
沈季文
translation_en:
… [fulfill] the merit of regulating and assisting, and only then does he dare to eat the ruler's emolument. Should his office be neglected while he merely eats the bread of idleness, he would regard it with fear; or should he receive rewards before results are achieved, he would likewise regard it with shame. How could such an attitude be acquired only today? It is precisely what was meant by the feeding at the very beginning of life. Shooting first and feeding afterward sets the expectation to be fulfilled: a loving father thereby nurtures his son and cultivates in advance the capabilities of a great man—this is the establishment of the target for a minister. Putting service first and salary afterward fulfills that expectation: a loyal minister thereby serves his ruler without losing the heart of a newborn infant—this is the embodiment of the teaching for a male. Observing the ritual shooting at birth, I know how loyalty is fostered. Great indeed is the timely significance of archery!

Ever since the learning of rectifying duty and illuminating the Way ceased to be discussed, the attraction of utilitarian gain has moved men deeply; this is simply because their aspirations are not fixed. Yu, Ji, Yi Yin, and the Duke of Zhou, as sages assisting sages, achieved brilliantly manifest meritorious deeds. Yet if we calmly examine what was meant by thinking of combining [the works of the three], thinking of a single common man or woman not receiving [the benefits of wise rule], and thinking of the hunger and drowning of all under Heaven, when were their aspirations ever not set upon Heaven, Earth, and the four quarters? For this reason they did not shrink from calloused hands and feet, nor did they spare themselves in anxious toil—how could it be a matter of profit and emolument! Therefore it is said: "Archery is the drawing out of one's own aspirations." This, again, is the doctrine of fixing one's aspirations.

"The Mutual Interaction Between Heaven and Man"

體一故也是作剴切奇古博雅宏邃雖漢儒策簡不過
矣宜錄
考試官右贊善許批尋常言天未有及此者
誦之悚然
考試官右中允何批以理著幾微立論而於
君之格天一致意焉董生之旨得□益明矣
夫天人一體相為感通其理至著而其幾至微
也人君奉天而為之子必以天之心為心天監
在下亦必以君之心為心君以天為心故其畏
民也乃所以畏天也天以君為心故其愛君也
乃所以愛民也天之愛民甚矣豈其使一人肆
於民上以從欲而滋亂必不然矣明君知此兢
兢然惟恐一失其道使天下之民或有不得其
所而獲戾于天是故遇災而思睹異而懼用能
反異為常變災為瑞天休滋至而福祚無疆也
漢董仲舒告其君首言天人相與之際夫天人
之際世儒論之蓋詳乃徒以理言疑於茫昧而

Comment by Associate Examiner, the metropolitan graduate (jinshi) Fang: That the mutual interaction of Heaven and humanity is called an "intersection" (ji) is because their substance is one. This composition is incisive and remarkably antique, erudite, refined, vast, and profound; even the policy tablets of the Han Confucians do not surpass it. It ought to be recorded.
Comment by Examiner, Right Admonisher Xu: Ordinary discussions of Heaven have never reached this level; reciting it fills one with awe.
Comment by Examiner, Right Companion He: It establishes its argument on the basis that the principle is manifest while the subtleincipience is minute, and focuses single-mindedly on the ruler's moving of Heaven. Through [this?], the purport of Master Dong [Zhongshu] becomes all the clearer.

Now, Heaven and humanity are of one substance, mutually responding and communicating; the principle of this is most manifest, while its subtle incipience is most minute. The ruler of men receives Heaven's mandate and acts as its Son, so he must take the mind of Heaven as his mind; Heaven looks down upon the world below, and likewise must take the mind of the ruler as its mind. Because the ruler takes Heaven as his mind, his standing in awe of the people is precisely how he stands in awe of Heaven; because Heaven takes the ruler as its mind, its loving the ruler is precisely how it loves the people. Heaven's love for the people is profound indeed! Would it ever allow a single man to act unrestrainedly above the people, indulging his desires and breeding disorder? Surely it is not so. The enlightened ruler knows this, and is cautiously fearful lest he once lose his Way, causing some among the people of the empire to fail to find their proper place and thereby incurring guilt before Heaven. Therefore, when he encounters calamities he reflects, and when he witnesses anomalies he is afraid; thus he is able to turn anomalies back into normality and transform calamities into auspicious signs, so that Heaven's blessings arrive in abundance and his good fortune and reign are boundless.

In the Han dynasty, when Dong Zhongshu advised his ruler, he spoke first of "the intersection of the mutual interaction between Heaven and humanity." title: 萬曆四年順天府鄉試錄
text:
無所指且天道遠人道邇安見其相與而稱際
焉今夫天積氣耳氣積而神靈聚焉氣之乘虛
無所不至故神之乘氣無所不通天畜於山澤
夫於天大象著之矣彼其下視蒼蒼猶是也人
之於天譬魚之於水由中達外無適而非是矣
日月之明不及於蔀屋而天盈焉雨露之潤不
及於巖石而天入焉故天也者人雖欲離之不
可得也不睹不聞隱微幽獨莫非天也故曰潜
雖伏矣亦孔之昭又曰上帝臨女無貳爾心由
===
是觀之天之與人甚於人之與人何也人與人
同類而體猶二也天與人同體則一而已燕臣
拊標而霜飛齊女籲號而風振匹夫匹婦尚然
況大君乎凡民之精神運於一家諸侯之精神
運於一國大君之精神運於一世故大君者一
世之人之所繫命也天既金畀以所覆蓋尤注
意焉大君與天同覆而合爲一體是故明廷臨
御深宮燕閒一言之是非一動之邪正不可謂
無與於天也日躔離合星軌順逆山川震寧年

Now, Heaven is nothing more than accumulated vital energy (qi), and where vital energy accumulates, spiritual efficacy gathers. As vital energy rides upon emptiness, there is nowhere it does not reach; therefore, as spirit rides upon vital energy, there is nothing it does not penetrate. That Heaven is stored within the mountain, and the marsh rises up to [?] Heaven—the Great Images of the Classic of Changes make this manifest; looking down from above at the vast azure, it is just the same. Man's relation to Heaven is like that of fish to water: reaching from the inside to the outside, wherever one goes, nothing is not this. The brightness of the sun and moon does not reach into adarkened hut, yet Heaven fills it; the moisture of rain and dew does not reach under overhanging crags, yet Heaven enters there. Therefore, even if man wished to separate himself from Heaven, it would be impossible. In what is unseen and unheard, in the hidden, subtle, and solitary, there is nothing that is not Heaven. Thus it is said: "Although it lies sunk and hidden, it is also exceedingly clear." And again it is said: "God on High looks down upon you; do not be duplicitous in your heart." Viewed from this perspective, the intimacy between Heaven and man is even greater than that between one person and another. Why is this? People are of the same kind as other people, yet their bodies are still two; Heaven and man share the same body, so they are simply one. When the minister of Yan beat his breast [?], frost flew in summer; when the woman of Qi cried out to Heaven, a fierce wind was stirred up. If it is thus even for common men and women, how much more so for the Great Sovereign! The spiritual energy of a commoner operates within a single family; the spiritual energy of a feudal lord operates within a single state; the spiritual energy of the Great Sovereign operates throughout a whole generation. Therefore, the Great Sovereign is the one upon whom the lives and destinies of the people of a whole generation depend. Since Heaven has wholly [?] entrusted to him all that it covers, it pays special attention to him. The Great Sovereign shares with Heaven the work of covering all things, uniting with it as a single body. Therefore, whether presiding in the bright court or resting at leisure in the deep palace, the rightness or wrongness of a single word, the crookedness or uprightness of a single action, cannot be said to have no bearing upon Heaven. title: 萬曆四年順天府鄉試錄
text:
穀登耗風雨之節不節寒暑之時不時不可謂
無與於人也何也一體故也盡性而參賛慎獨
而位育豈虛語哉且民者天之所生未有爲父
毋而不愛其所生者父母愛其所生故撫吾所
生吾喜焉殘吾所生吾怒焉九重之貴萬方之
富非徒以奉一人而已也爲能愛吾所生也此
其意可知也君道得則治而民生安君道失則
亂而民生不安故失道先告之以災害不省復
警之以恠異天之仁愛人君而欲止其亂也其
===
意可知也警告在天而轉移在人此天人之際
之所以可畏也自昔言天人者莫具於詩書矣
天視自我民視天聽自我民聽言天而徵於人
也昊天曰明及爾出王昊天曰旦及爾游衍言
人而徵於天也一秉心也何與於天曰昊天不
平一行政也何與於天曰昊天不惠天何聽納
曰辟言不信天何慮圖曰謀猶不臧民之鮮終
何以曰諶之難民之多辟何以曰牖之易湎酒
則曰天降威淫刑則曰天降罔夫非以一體之

punctuated: 穀登耗，風雨之節不節，寒暑之時不時，不可謂無與於人也。何也？一體故也。盡性而參賛，慎獨而位育，豈虛語哉！且民者，天之所生，未有爲父毋而不愛其所生者。父母愛其所生，故撫吾所生，吾喜焉；殘吾所生，吾怒焉。九重之貴，萬方之富，非徒以奉一人而已也，爲能愛吾所生也，此其意可知也。君道得則治，而民生安；君道失則亂，而民生不安。故失道，先告之以災害，不省，復警之以恠異。天之仁愛人君而欲止其亂也，其意可知也。警告在天，而轉移在人，此天人之際之所以可畏也。自昔言天人者，莫具於《詩》、《書》矣。「天視自我民視，天聽自我民聽」，言天而徵於人也；「昊天曰明，及爾出王。昊天曰旦，及爾游衍」，言人而徵於天也。一秉心也，何與於天？曰：「昊天不平。」一行政也，何與於天？曰：「昊天不惠。」天何聽納？曰：「辟言不信。」天何慮圖？曰：「謀猶不臧。」民之鮮終，何以曰諶之難？民之多辟，何以曰牖之易？湎酒則曰「天降威」，淫刑則曰「天降罔」。夫非以一體之
translation_en:
…the abundance or scarcity of annual harvests, the regularity or irregularity of wind and rain, and the timeliness or untimeliness of cold and heat cannot be said to have nothing to do with humankind. Why is this? Because they are a single body. Fully realizing one's nature to assist in the transforming and nourishing powers of Heaven and Earth, and being watchful over oneself when alone so that Heaven and Earth maintain their proper positions and all things are nourished—how could these be empty words!

Moreover, the people are that which Heaven has given birth to, and there have never been parents who do not love their own offspring. Because parents love their offspring, when someone nurtures my offspring, I rejoice; when someone harms my offspring, I am angered. The exalted status of the ninefold palace and the wealth of the myriad regions are not merely to serve a single man; they are granted because he is able to love what Heaven has given birth to. From this, Heaven's intention can be known. When the way of the ruler is attained, there is order and the people's livelihood is secure; when the way of the ruler is lost, there is disorder and the people's livelihood is insecure. Therefore, when he loses the way, Heaven first notifies him with calamities; if he does not examine himself, it further warns him with strange anomalies. That Heaven benevolently loves the ruler of men and wishes to stop his disorder—from this, its intention can be known. Warnings and notifications rest with Heaven, while turning the situation around rests with man; this is why the interaction between Heaven and man is to be held in awe.

Since antiquity, discussions of Heaven and man have nowhere been more complete than in the Book of Odes (Shi) and the Book of Documents (Shu). "Heaven sees as my people see; Heaven hears as my people hear"—this speaks of Heaven and verifies it through man. "Great Heaven is intelligent, and is with you in all your goings; Great Heaven is clear-sighted, and is with you in your wanderings and indulgences"—this speaks of man and verifies it through Heaven. Merely holding a state of mind—what has that to do with Heaven? Yet it says, "Great Heaven is unjust." Merely carrying out administration—what has that to do with Heaven? Yet it says, "Great Heaven is unkind." How does Heaven listen and accept? Yet it says, "Correct words are not believed." How does Heaven deliberate and plan? Yet it says, "The counsels and plans are not good." When the people rarely have a good end, why does it say that Heaven is hard to rely upon? When the people have many perversities, why does it say that Heaven easily leads them on? Of indulgence in wine, it says "Heaven sends down its terrors"; of excessive punishments, it says "Heaven sends down its net." Is this not because of their being a single body…

□是故帝懷明德曰監在茲天之與人以□
言配命順帝之則人之與天也天之與人常□
而不漏人之與天常燦而不殊明明赫赫達□
上下吉凶不僭去就無常是其際可畏也故其
德也曰馨聞其不德也曰穢彰其道得也曰啓
其衷其道失也曰奪其鑒其治也曰保定而俾
戬榖其亂也曰疾威而降鞠凶其興也曰眷顧
而式廓增其亡也曰棄絕而大命訖矣然而天
有定不定者何也世儒以爲天人之際固交相
===
勝也乃天亦曷嘗不定哉堯舜在上而蓂生鳳
儀此祥之正也夏商將亡而山頹川竭此災之
正也蓋亦有愛而警之者商戊之桑榖周成之
雷電是也有驕而絕之者後趙之蒼麟後魏之
白雉是也此災祥之變也故惠迪吉從逆凶積
善餘慶積不善餘殃在天未有不定者也災亦
或爲祥祥亦或爲災天命旣受我不敢知曰永
孚于休若天棐忱我亦不敢知曰終出于不祥
在人則未敢遽以爲定也實若草木應惟影響

translation_en: … [?] Therefore, when it is said that "the Lord on High cherishes bright virtue" and "His inspection is right here," this speaks of how Heaven relates to man through [?]; when it is said to "always match the Mandate" and "accord with the rules of the Lord on High," this speaks of how man relates to Heaven. Heaven's relation to man is ever [vast?] and lets nothing slip through; man's relation to Heaven is ever resplendent and admits no divergence. Bright and awe-inspiring, reaching [throughout] above and below, good fortune and calamity never err, and Heaven's favor comes and goes without constancy—such is the fearfulness of the juncture between Heaven and man. Thus, when a ruler is virtuous, it is said that his fragrant virtue is smelled on high; when he lacks virtue, it is said that his foulness becomes manifest. When he attains the Way, it is said that Heaven opens his inner mind; when he loses the Way, it is said that Heaven deprives him of his discernment. When there is order, it is said that Heaven protects and settles him, granting him every excellence and blessing; when there is disorder, it is said that Heaven is fierce in its wrath and sends down utter ruin. When a dynasty rises, it is said that Heaven looks upon it with favor and enlarges its domain; when it perishes, it is said that Heaven abandons and cuts it off, bringing the Great Mandate to an end. Yet why is it said that Heaven is sometimes settled and sometimes unsettled? Mundane scholars hold that at the juncture of Heaven and man, the two indeed alternately prevail over one another. But how has Heaven ever been unsettled? When Yao and Shun were on the throne, the calendar-pod plant grew and phoenixes came with stately bearing—this was the regular norm of auspicious omens. When the Xia and Shang dynasties were about to perish, mountains collapsed and rivers dried up—this was the regular norm of calamities. Indeed, there are also cases where Heaven loves a ruler and therefore warns him, such as the mulberry and grain tree growing together under Taiwu of Shang, or the thunder and lightning under King Cheng of Zhou; and there are cases where Heaven indulges a ruler in his arrogance so as to cut him off, such as the azure unicorn under the Later Zhao, or the white pheasant under the Later Wei—these are the variations of calamities and auspicious omens. Therefore, "following the right path brings good fortune, while following the perverse brings calamity," and "the family that accumulates goodness is sure to have an abundance of blessings, while the family that accumulates evil is sure to have an abundance of disasters"—with respect to Heaven, there has never been anything unsettled. Yet calamity may sometimes turn into an auspicious omen, and an auspicious omen may sometimes turn into calamity. As the Book of Documents says, "Even when the Mandate of Heaven has been received, I dare not know and say that it will forever abide in blessing; and even if Heaven aids sincerity, I likewise dare not know and say that it will end in misfortune"—with respect to man, one never dares rashly to consider it settled. translation_en:
…therefore it is said that "its principle is manifest." The mandate of rise and fall leaves not a hair's breadth in between, and the source of constancy and change is decided in an instant; therefore it is said that "its subtle triggers are minute." For this reason, when the worthy rulers of antiquity went a whole year without a calamity, they would say, "Has Heaven forgotten me?" And when various blessings appeared in succession, they would say, "By what virtue do I receive these?" It was not that they deliberately declined auspicious signs and courted calamities, but truly because the interaction between Heaven and man is to be held in awe. The ruler of men is the eldest son of Heaven. When one's parents love one, to rejoice and not forget it; when one's parents are angry with one, to toil and not bear resentment—this is the way of serving Heaven. Therefore, what is practiced below is clearly communicated above: when words are good, the planet retreats through the lunar lodges; when governance is cultivated, locusts depart the borders. If the head of a single commandery or princedom can achieve such sympathetic resonance, how much more so one who occupies a position above this?

Dong Zhongshu's (仲舒) main purport was derived from the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu). The Spring and Autumn Annals binds the king to Heaven and binds the first month of the year to the king, showing that Heaven and man form a single body. Where there is censure, calamities and harms are added; where there is abhorrence, prodigies and anomalies are visited upon them. Such is the nature of their mutual interaction. Alas, how awe-inspiring it is! Therefore, one who rules over men, even in times of flourishing foundations and supreme harmony, does not forget that calamities, harms, prodigies, and anomalies may arrive. Knowing that the Supreme Lord's favor rests upon virtue, standing in awe of the strictness of the common people below, being diligent in inquiry and learning so as to carry out the Way to the utmost, putting moral transformation first and punishments and penalties second, and honoring benevolence and righteousness above utilitarian profit—then Heaven and man will preserve one another and the altars of state will enjoy enduring peace. Thus it is said: "The matter lies simply in strenuous effort, and nothing more." When the Book of Odes (Shi) sets forth "Be reverent!" and the Book of Documents (Shu) admonishes "Exert yourselves!", both refer to strenuous effort.

…an Imperial edict to respectfully compose poems on the Painting of the Four Steeds of Emperor Chengzu Wen (Si jun tu) and present them upon completion.

Wang Shiqi 王士琦

Comment by Associate Examiner, Metropolitan Graduate (jinshi) Zhang 張: Solemn, dignified, clear, and thorough; by lodging admonition within eulogy, it vividly conveys sentiments of loyalty and devotion.

Comment by Examiner, Right Admonisher (you zanshan) Xu 許: Skillfully depicts the hardships of founding the dynasty; its sentiments are loyal, gentle, and praiseworthy, going beyond mere craftsmanship in parallel prose.

Comment by Examiner, Right Companion (you zhongyun) He 何: Continuous and overflowing sincerity and loyalty are fully revealed within its eulogizing narration; this is no casually composed piece.

On a certain day of the fifth month of the fourth year of the Wanli 萬曆 reign [1576], having humbly received the favor of Your Majesty bringing forth from the Inner Treasury the Painting of the Four Steeds of Emperor Chengzu Wen to show to Your servant, I respectfully obey the Imperial edict to reverently compose poems and present them.

Humbly I reflect: With divine martiality handing down his grand counsels, he specially commissioned paintings of the dragon breeds from his campaigns in the four directions; with reverent culture continuing the imperial line, You command songs to be sung of the illustrious achievements of a thousand years. … difficult to compose court odes and dynastic hymns. How dare I offer verses in response to the imperial decree, or take this occasion to convey admonition? Your servant, in utmost fear and trepidation, bows his head to the ground and submits these words:

I venture to reflect that among the five materials, none can dispense with weapons, and warfare first had its foundation at Zhuolu; among the three uses of steeds, none compares to riding horses, and the regulations for taming them were perfected in the rites of breaking colts. Yet auspicious creatures of the waters and essences of the stars emerge only in response to their appointed epoch; bearing patterned markings and submitting to the stable, they are not born except under a sage. Returning horses to pasture on Mount Hua, we praise the laying down of arms at Haojing; producing spirit-steeds from the Wowa River, we deride the composing of songs for the suburban sacrifices. Thus we hear of the reckless wanderings with the Eight Chargers, and also of the exhaustive expeditions of the Ershi General. When the bit is worn too long, the horse grows weary and control is lost; when arms are not laid to rest, one burns oneself with them.

Only our Dynasty has used Chinese ways to transform the barbarians, and thus through successive generations it has arrayed its armies and addressed its troops. Oh, august was Chengzu, who carried forward martial achievements! Indignant that warhorses were bred on the frontiers, he drove the hairy dragons to battle in the wilds. The six flying steeds he personally drove; the four chargers galloped in turn. Leaping on the Dragon Foal at Zhengba, his vanguard surpassed flashing lightning; rearing the Red Hare at Baigou, his momentum exceeded clap-of-thunder. Driving the Hualiu steed, he trampled flat Xiaohe; harnessing the Tenghuang courser, he galloped unrestrained across Lingbi. Piercing the ranks, they trampled down the elephants of Kunyang; charging the camps, they surpassed the fire-oxen of Jimo. Yet even when the миллиона-strong host had already turned their spears, a single warrior still wore his archer's thumb-ring and arm-guard. Their chests bathed in crimson blood—how could that merely be from a stray arrow's chance hit? Chasing the wind through military ramparts, did anyone ever see their frost-white hooves stumble even slightly? Their fierce spirit grew ever more ardent in the heat of battle; their vigorous frame strove to be first despite grievous wounds. Thus he founded extraordinary merits that shook the world, relying alike on their peerless, wondrous fleetness of foot. Thereupon he summoned the court painters to fully depict their surpassing…

… extraordinary talent, truly conforming in physiognomy to the classic diagrams, as vivid as when they galloped valiantly into battle against the enemy. Once the true dragons of the ninefold palace emerged, all ordinary horses throughout the ages were swept away into nothingness; were it not for the miraculous artistry of Cao Ba and Han Gan, how could they move the grooms and the Chamberlain for the Imperial Stud to such wistful admiration? Indeed, in quelling rebellion through martial prowess, this displays the hardships of founding the dynasty; and in contemplating danger while dwelling in peace, it already embodies the admonition against complacency in times of fullness and accomplishment.

When brought forth in the hands of the Directorate for Imperial Manufacturies, a rushing wind seems to rise from the unpainted silk; when wiped clean and viewed in the Imperial Archives, the attendants on left and right are refreshed and struck with awe in spirit. Imagining their vigorous cloud-treading stride, how could even a single speck of dust be startled into rising? Picturing them shaking their manes with a long neigh, ten thousand cavalrymen would surely fall back before them in terror. Hung high in the Unicorn Pavilion, their forms ought to be celebrated alongside the tiger-like warriors; displayed afar at Mount Langju, they would straightway rob the felt-wearing nomads of their very souls.

Furthermore, having received the imperial decree, I have been undeservedly entrusted with composing an appreciative inscription. Were I to leaf through the surviving manual of Bole, I would merely boast of the bones of a steed; having always been ignorant of Fei Chang's skill in charioteering, how could I properly eulogize these dragon-like mounts? Yet since the Eulogies of Lu (Lu song) contains the ode "Stout Horses" (Jiong), how would I dare perform the tune of the Pushao horse? And since the Admonition of the Gameskeeper (Yu zhen) can be recounted, how could I present the ballad of the Yellow Pool (Huangze)? For a loyal minister prizes using material things as a vehicle to offer up his devotion, and only an enlightened sovereign can perceive the shadow by observing the form. Surveying this resplendent great enterprise, how could one be without reverent and cautious care?

I reverently reflect that Your Majesty the Emperor rises preeminent above the multitude of things…

translation_en: …and grandly covers all living beings. In a time when shields, halberds, bows, and arrows have long been sheathed, even the birds, beasts, fishes, and turtles all follow their natural course. Emulating the galloping of the Former Kings and modeling Yourself on the striding of the Five Emperors, Your fragrant precedents have already been traced back through distant antiquity; expounding the virtue of the Progenitor and unfolding the achievements of the Ancestor, Your grand strategy is even more earnestly devoted to recounting the recent past. Happening to unroll the paintings and fix Your gaze upon them, You immediately issued a command that poems be presented. Were it not that founding and preserving share a single mind, who would remember the hundred battles fought through hardship and peril? Though the smoke of hearth fires extends for ten thousand li, You do not forget the thorough precautions of driving with rotten reins; though Your whip has subdued all the four borderlands, You remain mindful of the old affairs of being shot in the belt buckle. Indeed, taking warning when free from anxiety, You hope to hear fine words on preserving great peace; possessing greatness yet capable of humility, You do not prize extravagant panegyrics on dwelling in abundance. Your servant is ashamed of lacking the talent to compose while leaning against a horse, yet fortunate to have met the occasion of clinging to the Dragon. Having long pledged my service in galloping forward under the former reigns, I look precisely to today to be spurred on by the whip. Jiufang Yin (九方歅) is far in the past, so I examine the paintings closely, hesitating as the sundial's shadow shifts; yet the seven virtues of martial prowess reside therein, leading me to contemplate from afar the pacification of the realm in those bygone years. Whipping up wind and thunder and driving tigers and leopards before Him, the hundred spirits assuredly guarded and protected Him; yet braving arrows and stones and cutting through thorns and brambles, the Lord of Ten Thousand Chariots also approached the brink of peril. Moreover, if the gathering of divine steeds was such as this, then the heroes…

Yet in the principle of binding up mulberry roots before the rain, I may humbly align myself with the people of Zhou.

I humbly pray that Your Majesty will shine forth in virtue while storing up majesty, ordering the state with civil culture as the warp and military might as the woof; expand the great foundation by carrying on the ancestral work of laying the hall and raising the rafters, broadly seeking fine talents who can leap over clods like swift steeds; contemplate kingly measure so as to be pure as jade and gold, forever disdaining the frivolous amusement of horses rolling in the dust. Your servant is overcome with the utmost awe, trepidation, and earnest devotion in gazing up at Heaven and looking toward Your Sacred Majesty, and reverently presents this memorial along with the paintings for Your Majesty's information.

translation_en:
Zhang Xiaosun 張肖孫

Comment by Associate Examiner, Instructor (jiaoyu) Zhang: The exposition and response are detailed and clear, and the tireless words of admonition especially reveal the sincerity of his loyalty and devotion.

Comment by Associate Examiner, Instructor Jiang: The narration of matters is detailed and well-structured; at the end, it repeatedly sets forth the ideas of rectifying the mind and being watchful over oneself when alone, which is truly beneficial to the imperial self-cultivation.

Comment by Associate Examiner, Instructor Li: Throughout the essay, he recounts in turn the essentials of how the sage-kings since antiquity devoted themselves to learning, together with the transmission of the dynastic family learning of our Illustrious Ancestors. Its balance of detail and conciseness is well-structured, and to the very end of the piece he is especially earnest in advocating the doctrine of striving for practical substance. Surely he is one who truly looks to his sovereign to embody the learning of emperors and kings—is this gentleman not one who has long cherished a sincere devotion to guide his ruler to greatness!

Comment by Examiner, Right Admonisher (you zanshan) Xu: Whenever His Majesty studies the Classics and Histories, he pays close attention to the principles of governance. This is naturally what the lecturing officials have personally seen and heard, yet a rustic scholar from the countryside is able to recount it all point by point without error. At the close of the essay, he brings the argument back to rectifying the mind and being watchful over oneself when alone, which fully demonstrates his loyal sincerity; it is worthy of being presented to the throne.

text:
道化而有得者
愚生伏處蓬藿罕所識覩而執事詢以
主上聖學之宏深使鋪張揚厲其盛譬之繪天
測海何所擬其形容哉雖然
光華伊邇衣被獨先亦嘗得諸剽聞之萬一
矣敢援古為證以效管蠡之頌可乎夫帝
王之學與韋布不同何也內而砥礪身心
則養乎天德之精外而陶冶萬化則關乎
王道之大是故以古為憲以聖為準機執
===
其要功務其實而盛德大業從此出矣彼
資博洽獵英華終日從事而無與於身心
治理者殆非明君之以務學為急者也古
昔聖哲生而神靈莫如軒轅天錫勇智莫
如成湯然而功恒勵焉曰慓慓曰日新其

而志恒惕焉曰勤敬曰慎戒其勒諸戶牖
者可徵也商高宗命傅說以納誨而舟楫

punctuated:
道化而有得者。
愚生伏處蓬藿，罕所識覩，而執事詢以主上聖學之宏深，使鋪張揚厲其盛，譬之繪天測海，何所擬其形容哉？雖然，光華伊邇，衣被獨先，亦嘗得諸剽聞之萬一矣，敢援古為證，以效管蠡之頌可乎？夫帝王之學，與韋布不同，何也？內而砥礪身心，則養乎天德之精；外而陶冶萬化，則關乎王道之大。是故以古為憲，以聖為準，機執其要，功務其實，而盛德大業從此出矣。彼資博洽、獵英華，終日從事而無與於身心治理者，殆非明君之以務學為急者也。古昔聖哲，生而神靈莫如軒轅，天錫勇智莫如成湯，然而功恒勵焉，曰「慓慓」、曰「日新」，其銘諸輿盤者可鏡也；亶聰明莫如武王，然而志恒惕焉，曰「勤敬」、曰「慎戒」，其勒諸戶牖者可徵也。商高宗命傅說以納誨，而舟楫鹽梅之喻，愈望愈隆，安得不為中興之令…
translation_en:
…who has been nourished by the transforming influence of the Way and gained something from it.

As an ignorant student living in seclusion among weeds and brambles, there is little I have known or witnessed. Yet Your Honor asks about the vastness and profundity of His Majesty's sage learning, bidding me to elaborate upon and extol its flourishing state. This is like trying to paint the heavens or fathom the ocean—how could I possibly find anything to compare with its features? Even so, since the imperial radiance is near at hand and we are the very first to be clothed in its grace, I have also managed to catch one part in ten thousand from what I have heard in passing. May I venture to cite antiquity as evidence in order to offer praise as limited as viewing the sky through a tube or measuring the sea with a calabash?

Now, the learning of emperors and kings differs from that of commoners in coarse cloth; why is this? Inwardly, it refines body and mind, thereby nourishing the essence of Heavenly virtue; outwardly, it molds the myriad transformations, thereby bearing upon the greatness of the Kingly Way. Therefore, taking antiquity as one's model and the sages as one's standard, grasping the essentials in its pivotal mechanisms and striving for substance in its achievements—from this, glorious virtue and great enterprise emerge. As for those who rely on broad erudition and hunt for literary flowers, busying themselves all day long with matters that have no bearing on self-cultivation or governance, that is scarcely what an enlightened ruler treats as urgent in devoting himself to learning.

Among the圣 sages and wise kings of antiquity, in being born divine and灵 numinous none equaled Xuanyuan [the Yellow Emperor], and in being endowed by Heaven with courage and wisdom none equaled Cheng Tang [Tang of Shang]. Yet they constantly exerted themselves in their efforts, speaking of being "tremblingly cautious" and of "daily renewal"—what they inscribed upon their carriages and washbasins can serve as a mirror. In genuine intelligence, none equaled King Wu of Zhou, yet in his will he remained ever vigilant, speaking of "diligent reverence" and "careful warning"—what he engraved upon his doors and windows can serve as proof. Gaozong of Shang commanded Fu Yue to offer instruction, and through the metaphors of the boat and oars and of salt and plum, the more he hoped for, the more exalted it became; how could he not become a fine… [ruler of restoration?]

… ruler of a dynastic revival? King Cheng of Zhou invited his assembled ministers to take counsel at the outset of his reign, and his thoughts of continuing the work of his ancestors' court and bearing that heavy burden on his shoulders were expressed again and again with the utmost earnestness—how could he not have become a worthy ruler who succeeded to the throne? From the eras of decline onward, learning lacked a fundamental source and effort was not earnestly carried to the utmost. There were indeed cases where a single action happened to be good or a single point of conduct was praised as enlightened; yet if one must discuss the flourishing virtue of the Yellow Emperor, Yu Shun, and the Three Dynasties, how could those later rulers even be worthy of mention?

I reflect upon how our Grand Progenitor, Emperor Gao (the Hongwu Emperor), was endowed by Heaven with godlike intelligence and thoroughly analyzed the Classics and the Histories. For instance, he explicated the "Great Plan" (Hongfan) to clarify the inner intentions of Jizi and Yu the Great; he explicated the Analects (Lunyu) to correct the errors of the Song-dynasty Confucians; he lectured on the Book of Changes (Zhouyi) with Zhu Shan, lectured on the Great Learning (Daxue) with Wang Yi, lectured on the Mencius (Mengzi) with Xu Cunren, and lectured on the various Histories with men such as Song Lian and Liu Sanwu—more than can easily be recounted in full. And as for the precision and accuracy of his critical judgments, were not the meanings left unexpressed by past sages thereby brilliantly illuminated?

Sage after sage succeeded one another, transmitting and guarding one and the same Way. The Ancestor of Accomplishment, Emperor Wen (the Yongle Emperor), composed the Method of the Mind in Sagely Learning (Shengxue xinfa), wherein the admirable instructions of all antiquity were gathered; the Benevolent Ancestor, Emperor Zhao (the Hongxi Emperor), composed the Direct Pointers to the Various Classics (Zhujing zhizhi), wherein the subtle words of the Six Classics were expounded; the Exemplary Ancestor, Emperor Chun (the Chenghua Emperor), composed the Mirror for Rulers Through the Ages (Lidai junjian), whereby models of good and warnings against evil were made manifest; and the Epochal Ancestor, Emperor Su (the Jiajing Emperor), composed the Admonition on Reverence and Unity (Jingyi zhen) and the Commentary on the Five Admonitions (Wuzhen zhu), whereby …

text:
明聖之述作以備嗚呼盛哉天啓我
皇上禀聰明首出之資懋自強不息之學朝經
而暮史左圖而右書義理之涵養既深
聖心之超悟彌至有因論政遂發明經旨者如
罷元宵燈火而舉有備無患之類是已有
因論史遂商諏治道者如講董宣彊項而
欲貴戚守法之類是已此與
聖祖之談經何異丹扆箴既嘗書
進矣必
===
命箋註其詞而忠讜若親乎辰告大寶箴既嘗
熟復矣必
命訓釋其義而諷喻悉徹於
淵衷此與
列聖之纂訓奚殊於時輔臣慶
聖聰之罕譬則以一語一藥申說命之篇
明主感良弼之開陳則以小心虛心暢蘊古之
旨一德交修精神流貫豈非納誨訪落之
再見哉且我

translation_en: …the writings of the enlightened sages were thereby made complete. Oh, how magnificent! Heaven has opened the way for Our Emperor, who, endowed with supremely intelligent and preeminent gifts, devotes himself to unceasing self-strengthening learning—studying the Classics by morning and histories by evening, with charts to his left and books to his right. As his cultivation in moral principles has grown deep, the transcendent comprehension of his imperial mind has become ever more complete. There are instances where, in discussing governance, he has brought to light the meaning of the Classics—such as discontinuing the Lantern Festival illuminations and citing the maxim "where there is preparedness there is no disaster." There are also instances where, in discussing history, he has deliberated upon the way of governance—such as lecturing on Dong Xuan's (董宣) unyielding neck and desiring that imperial relatives by marriage abide by the law. How does this differ from the Sacred Ancestor's discussions of the Classics? Once the Admonitions for the Cinnabar Screen (Dan'yi zhen) had been written out and presented, he insisted on commanding that its words be annotated, so that its loyal and forthright counsel seemed like timely admonitions heard in person; once the Admonitions on the Great Treasure (Dabao zhen) had been thoroughly reviewed, he insisted on commanding that its meaning be explicated, so that its remonstrances and allegories penetrated completely into the depths of his imperial heart. How does this differ from the compiled instructions of the Successive Sages? At this time, the Grand Secretaries, celebrating the rare discernment of the Imperial sagacity, elaborated upon the "Charge to Yue" (Yue ming) chapter with the phrase "every word a medicine"; and the enlightened sovereign, moved by the expositions of his worthy aides, drew out the import of "accumulating the ancient" through "carefulness and an open mind." With single-minded virtue they cultivate one another, their spirit flowing in mutual communion—is this not a reappearance of accepting instruction and consulting at the outset of a reign? translation_en:
… His Majesty not only pursues learning that matches the footsteps of the Shang and Zhou dynasties, but indeed also possesses the determination to become like Yao and Shun. Therefore, the great principles and great laws of the Two Emperors and Three Kings, which are the grand plans for governing the empire, are written in large characters and displayed in the palace halls; the twelve matters from "Revering Heaven" to "Economizing on Expenditures," which are the urgent tasks of governing the empire, are inscribed on hanging plaques and placed to the right of the throne. Even the inscriptions on carriages, washbasins, doors, and windows of antiquity—how could they surpass these? Foolish as I am, I am fortunate to be born in this age and to be one of its people; indeed, I scarcely have enough time to immerse myself in the transformative influence of the Way, so what could I possibly contribute to aid His Majesty's sacred self-cultivation? If I must speak, may I then draw out and elaborate the doctrine of grasping the essential and attending to the substantive, offering it as a humble gift like wild celery or warming in the sun?

In the past, Dong Zhongshu 董仲舒 once urged his ruler to establish sincerity within and carry it out in practice, asking how he would then differ from the Three Kings. The achievement he spoke of was by no means small, yet it amounted to nothing more than rectifying the mind in order to rectify the court, and extending this to the hundred officials and the myriad people. Wang Ji 王吉 once wished to establish a long-range policy for ten thousand generations and raise his enlightened ruler to the flourishing height of the Three Dynasties. The effect he envisioned was by no means short-reaching, yet it amounted to nothing more than saying that when a sage ruler acts alone in the recesses of the palace, if he gets it right the whole empire praises him, and if he gets it wrong the whole empire talks of it. This being so, is not rectifying the mind the essential point of sage learning? And is not vigilance in solitude the substantive practice of rectifying the mind? translation_en: … within lacks the mind of Yao and Shun, and yet desires to achieve the governance of Yao and Shun in what is applied to administration, that is impossible to attain." Great indeed are the August Words! From this we know that expounding the Classics and Histories is merely a secondary thread. Emperor Chengzu's instruction to Xie Jin 解縉 said: "When the mind can be tranquil and empty, it responds as affairs arrive; when affairs depart, it is like a clear mirror or still water, and naturally all is purely Heavenly Principle." Unified indeed is the August Mind! From this we know that compiling instructions and canons is likewise only a subsidiary matter. In short, by savoring the Sacred Instructions, the profound essence of the Two Ancestors (Taizu and Chengzu) can be known; and by citing the Two Ancestors, the profound essence of the Three Ancestors (Renzong, Xuanzong, and Xiaozong) can be known. This is the family model of the ruling house, and it is also the method of the mind. Has Your Sacred Brilliance ever cherished it in your breast or not? Seeking ever further: the admonitions inscribed on carriages and washbasins may not need to be set up, yet "not approaching [sensual pleasures]" and "not amassing [wealth]" are what ought to be obeyed; the warnings on doors and windows may not need to be displayed, yet "reverence prevailing" and "righteousness prevailing" are what ought to be striven for. When those below offer counsel, does it truly stem from "opening the mind" and "enriching the mind"? Then Your Majesty ought to match it by being humble in will and timely in diligence. When the Sovereign above takes counsel at the beginning of his rule, are there truly those who "show me how to display virtuous conduct"? Then Your Majesty ought to bring it to completion through daily progress and monthly advance. …

translation_en:
The Great Court is solemn indeed; yet can there be no moments when the Grand Tutors and Grand Guardians are not in attendance and the canons and instructions are not close at hand? Then there are the inscriptions beside the throne: by using what meets the eye to alert the mind, it is fitting to experience and embody them without sparing any effort. The gathering and heeding of counsel is broad indeed; yet can there be no moments when remonstrance and deliberation do not reach him and corrective admonitions are not heard? Then there are the admonitions to be pondered repeatedly: by using them for quiet contemplation and inward self-examination, it is fitting to receive them graciously just as if face to face. What is handed down from forebears and modeled on institutional charters need not be identical in outward form, so long as one seeks genuine and earnest practical achievement; honoring what one hears and practicing what one knows need not be identical in outward form, so long as one hopes solely for real efficacy in body and mind. Then we shall see glorious virtue and the great enterprise daily renewed and richly abundant. Should someone say that in the near term this is insufficient to manifest the resplendent light of our Illustrious Ancestors, or that in the long term it is insufficient to equal the lofty course of the august sovereigns of antiquity, how could this humble one believe it?

title: 萬曆四年順天府鄉試錄
text:
帝王之治天下有萬世不易之法有與時
變易之宜變易者所以善成其不易者也
夫法之始立也以為如是足以治矣方其
草創固未暇備或為法雖善而歷久則窮
於是有因革損益焉以補其所未備而通
其所已窮要在與時宜之無失其初立法
之意而後可以長治此之謂善守法蓋自
唐虞以來有典謨有典則其法尚畧惟周
之六典為詳自漢晉以來有故事有會要
===
其法漸煩惟唐之六典為約若夫兼總周
官折衷唐制定一代之章程垂萬年之法
守則
大明會典是已頃
勅輔臣開局命官分曹受事接弘治壬戌之舊
籍裁嘉靖己酉之新編甚盛舉也執事者
方載筆其間奉
明天子德意與賢公卿討論承學固陋何辱問
焉雖然嘗聞之矣周以六官綱紀天下至

translation_en: In the governance of the empire by sovereigns and kings, there are laws that remain unchanging for ten thousand generations, and there are adaptations that change with the times. That which changes is the means by which to bring to perfection that which does not change. When laws are first established, they are considered sufficient to bring about order as they are. Yet at their initial creation, there is naturally no leisure to make them exhaustive; or else, though the laws are good, after a long passage of time they become exhausted. Thus there are continuities, reforms, reductions, and additions, in order to supplement what was not yet complete and to unblock what has reached an impasse. The essential point lies in adapting them to the times without losing the original intent behind establishing the laws, after which enduring order can be achieved; this is what is called being skilled at upholding the laws. Indeed, since the eras of Tang [Yao] and Yu [Shun], there were canons and counsels, and there were statutes and standards, yet their laws were still sketchy; only the Six Canons (Liudian) of the Zhou were detailed. Since the Han and Jin dynasties, there were precedents (gushi) and institutional compendia (huiyao), and their laws grew increasingly cumbersome; only the Six Canons of the Tang (Tang liudian) was concise. As for comprehensively gathering the Offices of Zhou (Zhouguan) and striking a balance with the Tang institutions, fixing the regulations of an entire era and handing down legal standards for ten thousand years, that is none other than the Collected Statutes of the Great Ming (Da Ming huidian). Recently, an imperial decree ordered the Grand Secretaries to open a bureau and appointed officials to divide into sections and take up the task, continuing the old text of the renxu year of the Hongzhi era (1502) and editing the new compilation of the jiyou year of the Jiajing era (1549)—a truly magnificent undertaking! You, the examiners, are just now wielding your brushes in its midst, upholding the virtuous intentions of the enlightened Son of Heaven and deliberating with worthy high ministers; as a shallow and ignorant junior scholar, how could I be worthy of your condescending inquiry? title: 萬曆四年順天府鄉試錄
text:
於柞木薙草各有司存而分職率屬大小
相維以聽於六官者其大體不可易也唐
以三省綱紀天下至於凾案裝潢各有司
存而分職率屬大小相維以聽於三省者
其大體不可易也
國家以九卿綱紀天下六部則周官也院司
寺監則唐制也舉百司庶務大小相維而
囊括於九卿者其大體不可易也譬治絲
者縷析之而綜握之雖棼不亂蓋

translation_en: … down to the officials for clearing trees and cutting weeds, each had its own responsible office; yet in dividing duties and leading subordinates, with great and small mutually connected so as to answer to the Six Offices, its grand framework could not be altered. The Tang governed the realm through the Three Departments (San sheng), and even down to the tasks of document cases and scroll mounting, each had its own responsible office; yet in dividing duties and leading subordinates, with great and small mutually connected so as to answer to the Three Departments, its grand framework could not be altered. Our Dynasty governs the realm through the Nine Chief Ministers (Jiu qing): the Six Ministries (Liu bu) follow the Offices of Zhou, while the Censorate, Offices, Courts, and Directorates follow the system of the Tang. Taking all the myriad affairs of the hundred offices, with great and small mutually connected and encompassed under the Nine Chief Ministers, its grand framework cannot be altered. It is like one who manages silk threads: separating them strand by strand while grasping them in the heddle, so that even if tangled, they do not fall into disorder. Indeed, the High Emperor (Gao Huangdi, i.e., Emperor Taizu) examined antiquity to establish the institutions, deciding from His Sacred Mind to compile the Functions of the Various Offices (Zhusi zhizhang); and Emperor Xiaozong first commanded Confucian臣 (literati officials) to classify and append to it the various books promulgated by the throne and the precedents accumulated over the years, creating the Collected Statutes of the Great Ming (Da Ming huidian). This canonical statute was what the Imperial Ancestor revised and settled in his later years, and what the Successive Sages embellished in subsequent eras; it is utterly clear and complete. As for the new compilation of the jiyou year (1549), there is no way for me to have seen or recorded it. Yet from the Hongzhi era to the present, the reigns have changed through Four Sages and the years have exceeded six twelve-year cycles (seventy-two years); the regulations and precedents increase daily while adherence to the law grows daily more confused—is this not the time for revision and adjustment? title: 萬曆四年順天府鄉試錄
text:
秘府之藏百司之守其義例則
孝皇勅旨在于復何言無已請即壬戌之舊質
以周唐之典畧陳一二可乎夫紀載者莫
先於體裁莫要於綱目莫纖悉於沿革事
宜弘治
勅曰遵
祖製稽國史言體裁也官職制度爲綱事物名
數儀文等級爲目言綱目也損益同異據
事繫年言沿革事宜也周禮而後惟唐六
===
典宋祁所謂精密簡要曾鞏所謂文不煩
而實備者故當時王鏊欲倣以爲式然諸
司職掌雖不考周禮而暗與周合尚何論
唐亦各一世之法何必文武之方策而後
可布哉愚以爲雖周亦不必倣也此所謂
體裁者也周禮一書設官爲綱分職爲目
六官則冢宰爲綱五官爲目一官則長爲
綱屬爲目有一職之綱如小宰曰掌建邦
之宮刑小司徒曰掌建邦之教法是已有

translation_en:
…the holdings of the Imperial Library and the regulations maintained by the hundred offices; and as for its guiding principles and editorial rules, the imperial edict of Emperor Xiaozong is extant—what more need I say? If I must speak, may I take the old edition of the renxu year [1502], examine it against the canons of the Zhou and Tang dynasties, and briefly set forth a point or two?

In any compilation of records, nothing comes before overall structure, nothing is more essential than headings and subheadings, and nothing requires more minute detail than historical development and practical administration. The Hongzhi edict states, "Follow the ancestral institutions and consult the dynastic histories"—this refers to overall structure; "Make official titles and institutional systems the main headings, and make specific affairs, numerical categories, ritual forms, and grades of rank the subheadings"—this refers to headings and subheadings; "Where there are additions, reductions, similarities, or differences, attach the events to their respective years"—this refers to historical development and practical administration.

After the Rites of Zhou (Zhouli), there was only the Six Canons of the Tang (Tang liudian), which Song Qi宋祁 called "precise, thorough, concise, and essential," and which Zeng Gong曾鞏 described as "unencumbered in wording yet complete in substance." Thus, at the time, Wang Ao王鏊 wished to imitate it as a model. Yet although the Duties of All Offices (Zhusi zhizhang) did not consult the Rites of Zhou, it tacitly accords with the Zhou; what need is there even to speak of the Tang? Each era has its own laws for its generation; why must one have the wooden and bamboo tablets of Kings Wen and Wu before a system can be promulgated? In my humble opinion, even the Zhou need not be imitated. This is what is meant by overall structure.

In the Rites of Zhou as a book, the establishment of offices serves as the main headings, and the division of duties serves as the subheadings. Among the Six Offices, the Grand宰 (zhongzai, Minister of State) is the main heading and the other five offices are the subheadings; within a single office, the chief is the main heading and the subordinates are the subheadings. There is the main heading of a single office's duty, such as when the Vice Minister of State (xiaozai) is said to "take charge of establishing the palace penalties of the state," or when the Vice Minister of Education (xiao situ) is said to "take charge of establishing the educational laws of the state." text:
一事之綱如八法曰治官府八則曰治都
鄙是也今會典亦暗與之合部以司分司
以事分事有綱綱有目而目之中又有分
類有附見焉周禮以公孤非備官不列而
列六卿會典亦以師保爲加官不列而列
九卿若唐則併列之且旣有三省有三師
又益以三公何爲乎執事謂周唐建官不
同會典實本周官第宜仍舊編益新事是
也此所謂綱目者也會典之以行人次禮
===
部也本周禮春官有大小行人之屬也其
以中書六科先大理也本唐三省有中書

This is what is meant by headropes and mesh-eyes. translation_en:
… Hereditary Consorts (Nüyü), Female Scribes (Nüshi), and Minor Palace Attendants (Neixiaochen), while the Tang had Eunuch Officials (Neiguan), Palace Women Officials (Gongguan), and the Palace Domestic Service (Neishi [sheng] [?]). Why was this? Because the realm was regarded as a single family, and the palace and the government administration formed a single body. Today, in the various Directorates and Bureaus of the Inner Court, the offices have fixed quotas of personnel and the personnel have fixed duties. Might we not request that they be registered together and appended according to the matters they handle?

The Ministry of Revenue records the receipts from tribute and taxes, yet lacks the figures for disbursements within and without the capital; the Bureau of Operations records the names of camps and forts, yet lacks accounts of the strategic topography of choke points and vital zones; the frontier regions have established Defense Commands and garrisons, yet lack records of the territories assigned for divided protection and demarcated defense. The annual provisions for local and auxiliary troops are an enormous expenditure, yet they are glossed over and not preserved; the Branch Court of the Imperial Stud and the Pasturage Office are specialized agencies, yet they are merely appended rather than given their own entries. As for the increase and decrease of arable land and registered households, and the number of princely stipends and civil and military personnel—might we not request that all of these be registered in full, with their origins and causes clearly set forth?

Among state affairs, there are some that are enshrined in the foremost statutes and actively enforced in the present age; there are others that were obstructed after a long time, or proved unworkable as soon as they were tried; and there are even those that were merely temporary stopgap measures, never part of the regular system, or that were approved by chance in response to a memorialized request, yet in fact violate established norms. To record them all indiscriminately in chronological order, without any distinction of validity, merely enables pettifoggers to manipulate the rules for their own ends and meddlers to recklessly introduce confusing changes. Might we not request that within each category, those statutes that are codified and currently in force be elevated as the main headings, while the rest are either deleted or [abridged?], appearing only as appended notes for reference?

之視今猶今之視昔吾安能必數十年後
不又有因革損益今之所因革損益者哉
要以與時宜之無失
祖宗之初意以善成其不易者而已易窮則變
變則通通則久與詩書所稱成憲舊章何
悖抑愚又聞之弘治去洪武僅百四十年
耳是書所載土田戶口日減

後宜多也而顧少此必有繇矣且以日減

translation_en:
…even one part in ten thousand? This is what is meant by the appropriate measures for institutional continuity and change. Alas! Future generations will look upon the present just as the present looks upon the past. How can we be certain that several decades from now there will not again be those who retain, abolish, diminish, or augment what we in the present have retained, abolished, diminished, or augmented? The essential point is simply to adapt appropriately to the times without losing the original intentions of the Imperial Ancestors, thereby skillfully fulfilling what is immutable. The Book of Changes says: "When a series of changes has run all its course, another change ensues. When it obtains free course, it will continue long." How does this contradict the "established constitutions" and "ancient statutes" praised in the Book of Odes and the Book of Documents?

Moreover, I, in my ignorance, have heard this: the Hongzhi era was separated from the Hongwu era by a mere one hundred and forty years, yet as recorded in this book, the acreage of arable land and the number of households and mouths decreased daily, while the stipends of imperial princes and the quota of civil and military officials increased daily—not merely tenfold or a hundredfold. How did it come to this? At the founding, amid brambles and the wounds of war, the figures ought to have been small, yet on the contrary they were large; after land was cleared and the population multiplied, they ought to have been large, yet on the contrary they were small. There must be a reason for this. Furthermore, to take daily decreasing land and households to supply daily increasing princely stipends and official personnel—if this continues indefinitely, where will it end?

In the past, when Emperor Wen of the Han succeeded to the throne, he first asked how many criminal cases were decided each year, and how much money and grain entered and left the treasury. Now the Son of Heaven is in the prime of his youth. If he truly examines what is recorded in the Collected Statutes (Huidian), extends this inquiry broadly across all Six Ministries, and orders each to set forth the causes of surplus and deficit while itemizing appropriate measures for relief, then without stepping beyond the hall and stairs, the realm can be turned in the palm of his hand. Although these are borrowed words, they are quite pertinent to practical realities, and I humbly wish through you, the Examiners…

趙夢日
同考試官教諭姚批記聞精詳辭氣古雅
深得人臣任事之實異日必能肩重矣

治河亦難矣而往事卓有成效蓋任事得人而任任事者
專其任也是作敷答精詳錄之以告在事者
同考試官學正郝批四子任事之效條答
===

同考試官學正陳批任事之人固重任任
事之人尤重是作可謂知要矣
考試官右贊善許批任事在實心篇末數語可
以占子之自任矣佳士

任天下事計必有可觀者錄之非直以其文也

title: 萬曆四年順天府鄉試錄
text:
言盈庭貽譏作舍不任也蓋又有喜事之
臣夫喜事之臣攮袂先天下疑於任矣然
進極犀利退易缺折不任也蓋又有畏事
之臣夫畏事之臣藉口持天下疑於任矣
然首鼠牽制機會坐失不任也所謂任事
之臣者身事視君家事視國本是實心而
輔以才識乃罔不濟甚矣事之不易任也
平居而計天下以為吾盡吾心天下無難
為者及當事變紛綸四出而才力智識有
===
不暇給然後知事之難是故衆非獨是則
見憤忮而矜已衆是獨非則見妒媚而沮
物佹成而不取則以為失資佹敗而不棄
則以為賈禍利一害百以害掩利則見以
為拙成害一利百以利冒害則見以為迂

從後持之矣利或在易世之下未及其利

punctuated: 言盈庭，貽譏作舍，不任也。蓋又有喜事之臣。夫喜事之臣，攮袂先天下，疑於任矣；然進極犀利，退易缺折，不任也。蓋又有畏事之臣。夫畏事之臣，藉口持天下，疑於任矣；然首鼠牽制，機會坐失，不任也。所謂任事之臣者，身事視君，家事視國，本是實心，而輔以才識，乃罔不濟。甚矣，事之不易任也！平居而計天下，以為吾盡吾心，天下無難為者；及當事變，紛綸四出，而才力智識有不暇給，然後知事之難。是故衆非獨是，則見憤忮而矜已；衆是獨非，則見妒媚而沮物。佹成而不取，則以為失資；佹敗而不棄，則以為賈禍。利一害百，以害掩利，則見以為拙成；害一利百，以利冒害，則見以為迂。不在致期之間，未及其成而遽責焉，法吏從後持之矣；利或在易世之下，未及其利而先嘗焉，衆口從旁撓之矣。不幸而計失，曰「此固然耳」，既追論其首事而罪之；即幸…
translation_en: …fill the court with speeches, inviting the ridicule of building a house by the roadside—they do not shoulder responsibility. Then there are also ministers who delight in stirring up affairs. When a minister who delights in stirring up affairs rolls up his sleeves and puts himself ahead of the whole world, he seems to shoulder responsibility; yet though he is exceedingly sharp in advancing, he is easily chipped and broken in retreating—he does not shoulder responsibility. Then there are also ministers who shrink from affairs. When a minister who shrinks from affairs uses pretexts of preserving the empire, he seems to shoulder responsibility; yet he hesitates and holds back like a rat peering from its hole, sitting idly by as opportunities are lost—he does not shoulder responsibility. He who is truly called a minister who shoulders responsibility regards the ruler's affairs as those of his own person, and the state's affairs as those of his own family; grounded in this sincere heart and aided by talent and insight, there is nothing he cannot bring to success. How extreme is the difficulty of shouldering responsibility for affairs! In ordinary times, when one plans for the empire, one thinks that so long as one exhausts one's own heart, there is nothing in the world difficult to do; yet when one confronts changing crises breaking out in tangled profusion on all sides, and one's talent, strength, wisdom, and insight are insufficient to meet the demands, only then does one know the difficulty of affairs. Therefore, when the multitude thinks something wrong and he alone thinks it right, he is viewed as resentful, stubborn, and boastful of himself; when the multitude thinks something right and he alone thinks it wrong, he is viewed as jealous and obstructive of others. If success is nearly at hand and he does not seize it, he is considered to have forfeited an advantage; if failure is imminent and he does not abandon the course, he is considered to be courting disaster. Where there is one benefit and a hundred harms, and the harms outweigh the benefit, he is viewed as clumsy in bringing things to completion; where there is one harm and a hundred benefits, and he braves the harm for the sake of the benefits, he is viewed as impractical. If results do not fall within the stipulated time, and before completion is reached people abruptly demand an accounting, the legal officials are already at his back holding him to account; if the benefits perhaps lie generations in the future, and before the benefits are reached people first taste the difficulties, the mouths of the multitude are already at his side obstructing him. If, unfortunately, his plan fails, people say, "This was bound to happen," and they retroactively impeach him for initiating the affair and condemn him; even if, fortunately…

title: 萬曆四年順天府鄉試錄
text:
而計得曰此適然耳又苛論其細事而罪
之然則天下事終不可爲乎此執事感激
太息于任事之人以爲愈不易得也雖然
世未嘗無事事未嘗無人今夫北胡至難
禦也西羌至難安也逆藩至難取也洪河
至難治也然而趙李牧漢趙充國唐裴度
元賈魯優爲之此四臣者方其建議豈不
落落難合而竟成若券彼所以計之者審
矣牧之計在一大創虜故不日費饗士則
===
士不樂戰不收保則爲虜資不禁捕則虜
戒不來不有所委以誘之則虜不悉衆來
是其縱虜入者乃所以使不敢入也充國
計在招降罕幵令先零諸豪瓦解其處故
用兵則彼之交合而寇滋留田則我之力
省而威重用兵則人致我而勝負未可知
留田則我致人而可坐勝如彼則人臣之
利如此則社稷之福是其謂難踰度者乃
其度之深也度計在必討賊夫彰義三州

其度之深也度計在必討賊夫彰義三州
punctuated: 而計得，曰：「此適然耳。」又苛論其細事而罪之。然則天下事終不可爲乎？此執事感激太息于任事之人，以爲愈不易得也。雖然，世未嘗無事，事未嘗無人。今夫北胡至難禦也，西羌至難安也，逆藩至難取也，洪河至難治也；然而趙李牧、漢趙充國、唐裴度、元賈魯優爲之。此四臣者，方其建議，豈不落落難合？而竟成若券，彼所以計之者審矣。牧之計，在一大創虜，故不日費饗士則士不樂戰，不收保則爲虜資，不禁捕則虜戒不來，不有所委以誘之則虜不悉衆來。是其縱虜入者，乃所以使不敢入也。充國計在招降罕幵，令先零諸豪瓦解其處，故用兵則彼之交合而寇滋，留田則我之力省而威重；用兵則人致我而勝負未可知，留田則我致人而可坐勝。如彼則人臣之利，如此則社稷之福。是其謂難踰度者，乃其度之深也。度計在必討賊，夫彰義三州、
translation_en: …and the plan succeeds, they say, "This was merely a fluke," and then they harshly criticize trivial details in order to condemn him. If that is the case, can the affairs of the empire ultimately never be accomplished? This is why Your Excellency is moved to sigh deeply over men who shoulder responsibility, considering them ever more difficult to find. Even so, the world is never without affairs, and affairs are never without men to handle them. Now, the northern nomads are most difficult to fend off, the Western Qiang are most difficult to pacify, rebellious defense commands are most difficult to capture, and the great Yellow River is most difficult to control; yet Li Mu 李牧 of Zhao, Zhao Chongguo 趙充國 of Han, Pei Du 裴度 of Tang, and Jia Lu 賈魯 of Yuan handled them with ease. When these four ministers first proposed their plans, were they not aloof and hard for others to agree with? Yet in the end they succeeded as surely as holding a tally, because the way they calculated their plans was thorough. Li Mu's plan lay in dealing a single great blow to the raiders: therefore, if he did not spend daily to feast his soldiers, the soldiers would not be eager to fight; if he did not gather the people and livestock into fortifications, they would become supplies for the raiders; if he did not forbid capturing raiders, the raiders would be on guard and not come; and if he did not leave something behind to lure them, the raiders would not come in full force. Thus, his allowing the raiders to enter was precisely the means by which he made them dare not enter again. Zhao Chongguo's plan lay in inducing the Hanyan 罕幵 tribes to surrender and causing the various chieftains of the Xianling 先零 to disintegrate where they were: therefore, if he used military force, their alliances would unite and the bandits would multiply, whereas if he stationed troops to farm, our strength would be spared and our authority would carry weight; if he used military force, the enemy would draw us in and victory or defeat could not be known, whereas if he stationed troops to farm, we would draw the enemy in and could win without fighting. The former course would be to the advantage of a subject, while the latter course was a blessing to the altars of state. Thus, his saying that it was difficult to estimate from afar was in fact because his own estimation was profound. Pei Du's plan lay in 반드시 punishing the rebels: now, Zhangyi 彰義 was merely three prefectures, and…

title: 萬曆四年順天府鄉試錄
text:
元濟小豎子耳攻之四年不下何以示兩
河諸鎭諸鎭跋扈如故則賦擅不供兵連
不解何論師老財匱然則罷兵之利孰與
失兩河之害此度所以誓不與賊俱生也
魯計在一勞永逸夫故道難復大衆難聚
信如尚書成遵言然河歲决歲塞煩費無
已時今第起十七萬衆通道二百八十餘
里五閱月可成塞北河之害孰與疏南河
之利此魯所謂役不大興害不能已也何
===
者計定于先也蓋不待涉厲門馳金城臨
淮蔡黄陵白茅而是非成敗利害之機已
形於胸中矣是故任事之臣其先事而計
也循本揣末緣表察裏規畫一室而周四
海之外措注旬日而豫千百世之後未萌
若睹未習若素非嘗試而漫爲之也其計
定而行也見不可外移勢不可中格怨有
不避勞有不辭毁譽不驚死生不貳及其
成也上下宴如社稷蒙其利而已不有其

translation_en:
… [Wu] Yuanji 吳元濟 was merely a petty brat. If after attacking him for four years we could not take him down, what would that show to the various Defense Commands of the Two River regions [Hebei and Henan]? If those commands remained as recalcitrant as before, they would usurp revenues without paying tribute and warfare would drag on without end—what need would there be to speak of troops growing exhausted and finances being depleted? That being so, how could the advantage of halting the campaign compare to the harm of losing the Two River regions? This is why [Pei] Du 裴度 swore not to live under the same sky as the rebels.

As for [Jia] Lu's 賈魯 plan, it lay in making one great effort to secure permanent ease. Now, that the old course of the river was difficult to restore and a great multitude difficult to assemble was indeed just as Minister (shangshu) Cheng Zun 成遵 said. Yet the Yellow River breached its banks every year and had to be plugged every year, causing endless trouble and expense. Now, simply by mobilizing a force of 170,000 men to open a channel of more than 280 li, the work could be completed in five months. How could the harm of damming the northern river compare to the benefit of dredging the southern river? This is what Lu meant by saying, "Unless the corvée project is undertaken on a grand scale, the harm cannot be stopped."

Why was this? Because their plans were settled beforehand. Indeed, they did not have to wait until they reached Yanmen 鴈門 [written 厲門], galloped to Jincheng 金城, overlooked Huai 淮 and Cai 蔡, or stood at Huangling 黄陵 and Baimao 白茅 before the pivotal mechanisms of right and wrong, success and failure, benefit and harm had already taken shape in their minds.

Therefore, when a minister who shoulders responsibility formulates his plans prior to action, he traces the root to gauge the branches, examines the exterior to discern the interior, devises his schemes within a single chamber yet encompasses all beyond the four seas, and arranges matters over ten days yet makes provision for hundreds and thousands of generations to come. He sees what has not yet sprouted as though witnessing it before his eyes, and handles what he has not yet practiced as though long accustomed to it; he does not merely make a tentative trial or act recklessly. Once his plan is settled and he puts it into action, his judgment cannot be swayed from outside, nor can his momentum be blocked midway. There are resentments he does not shun and toils he does not decline; he is unshaken by slander or praise, and unwavering before life or death. And when he succeeds, superior and inferior alike enjoy peace, the altars of state receive the benefit, while he himself does not claim the…

title: 萬曆四年順天府鄉試錄
text:
功斯其爲真任事也已矣夫喜事似任任
事似畏而喜者生事者也畏者諉事者也
任者行所無事者也其重如弩持非畏也
其輕如鷙發非喜也此不可不察也牧充
國雖不先衆議而議者卒屈焉度若魯雖
與衆抗議而議者莫能難焉故好議非也
因而廢議亦非也議而能成何惡於議此
又不可不察也雖然有任事者有任任事
者今海内無事
===
天子垂意四顧不愛高位厚祿懸以待天下若
曰今獨不得牧充國爲將度往視師魯爲
河防使耳何憂北胡西羌東南山海之寇
河淮之漕哉愚戇不知忌諱竊以爲誠出
魯之計不爲行河者報罷乎出度之計不
爲言師老財匱者沮乎出充國與牧之計
辛武賢不見代乎縱虜不下廷尉乎即成
功不有以日費市租久留天誅議其後者
乎如此即令四臣在事掣肘無益也是故
